nodes.name: Foundations.Logic.FO.Proves.witness
nodes.doc:
**The witness lemma** (Henkin). Suppose the variable `x` occurs free neither in
the premises `Δ` nor in `∃y φ(y)`. If `Δ ⊢ ∃y φ(y)` and `Δ ∪ {φ(x)}` is
inconsistent, then `Δ` itself is inconsistent. So a fresh variable can always be
consistently declared to be a witness.
nodes.type:
∀ {L : Foundations.Logic.FO.Signature} {Δ : Foundations.Logic.FO.Theory L} {φ : Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula L}
  {x : Nat},
  (∀ (χ : Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula L), Δ χ → Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula.Fresh x χ) →
    Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula.Fresh x φ.ex →
      Δ ⊢₁ φ.ex →
        Δ.insert (φ.inst (Foundations.Logic.FO.Term.var x)) ⊢₁ Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula.bot →
          Δ ⊢₁ Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula.bot

nodes.name: Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.hartogs_theorem
nodes.doc:
**Hartogs' theorem.** For every type `α` there is an ordinal `h` that does not
inject into `α`, and it is the least such: an ordinal `o` lies in `h` exactly when
`o` injects into `α`, and every ordinal not injecting into `α` contains or equals `h`.
(The construction makes no choices; see the module docstring for what
`#print axioms` reports.)
nodes.type:
∀ (α : Type),
  ∃ h,
    h.IsOrdinal ∧
      (¬∃ f, Function.Injective f) ∧
        (∀ (o : Foundations.Sets.ZFSet), o.IsOrdinal → (o ∈ h ↔ ∃ f, Function.Injective f)) ∧
          ∀ (o : Foundations.Sets.ZFSet), o.IsOrdinal → (¬∃ f, Function.Injective f) → h = o ∨ h ∈ o

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.Categoricity.exists_rat_sq_between
nodes.doc:
Approximating a square from below by squares of rationals: if `0 < z` and `0 ≤ q < z²`
then some rational `r` with `0 ≤ r < z` has `q < r²`.
nodes.type:
∀ {K : Type} [inst : Lean.Grind.Field K] [inst_1 : LE K] [inst_2 : LT K] [inst_3 : Std.IsLinearOrder K]
  [inst_4 : Std.LawfulOrderLT K] [inst_5 : Lean.Grind.OrderedRing K],
  Foundations.Numbers.OF.Archimedean K →
    ∀ {z : K},
      0 < z →
        ∀ {q : Foundations.Numbers.Q},
          0 ≤ Foundations.Numbers.OF.ofRat q →
            Foundations.Numbers.OF.ofRat q < z * z →
              ∃ r,
                0 < Foundations.Numbers.OF.ofRat r ∧
                  Foundations.Numbers.OF.ofRat r < z ∧
                    Foundations.Numbers.OF.ofRat q < Foundations.Numbers.OF.ofRat r * Foundations.Numbers.OF.ofRat r

nodes.name: Foundations.Algebra.factorization_unique
nodes.doc:
**Uniqueness of factorisation.** In an integral domain in which every irreducible element
is prime — for instance any principal ideal domain — two factorisations into irreducibles of
associated elements agree up to order and units: if `∏ L = u · ∏ M` with `u` a unit, then for
every `x`, `L` and `M` contain equally many factors associated to `x`.
nodes.type:
∀ {R : Type u} [inst : Foundations.Algebra.CommRing R],
  Foundations.Algebra.IsDomain R →
    (∀ (p : R), Foundations.Algebra.Irreducible p → Foundations.Algebra.IsPrimeElt p) →
      ∀ (L M : List R) (u : R),
        (∀ (p : R), p ∈ L → Foundations.Algebra.Irreducible p) →
          (∀ (q : R), q ∈ M → Foundations.Algebra.Irreducible q) →
            Foundations.Algebra.IsUnit u →
              Foundations.Algebra.lprod L = u * Foundations.Algebra.lprod M →
                ∀ (x : R), Foundations.Algebra.countAssoc x L = Foundations.Algebra.countAssoc x M

nodes.name: Foundations.Algebra.dvd_count_of_saturated
nodes.doc:
**The tiling argument.** If a set `P` is a union of left cosets of `H` (i.e. closed under
right multiplication by elements of `H`), then `|H|` divides `|P|`. We peel off one coset
at a time: removing a coset from such a set leaves such a set, with `|H|` fewer elements.
nodes.type:
∀ {G : Type u} [inst : Foundations.Algebra.Group G] [inst_1 : Foundations.Algebra.FiniteType G]
  (H : Foundations.Algebra.Subgroup G) (n : Nat) (P : G → Prop),
  Foundations.Algebra.FiniteType.count P = n →
    (∀ (a h : G), P a → h ∈ H → P (a * h)) → (Foundations.Algebra.FiniteType.count fun x => x ∈ H) ∣ n

and is consistent together with the finite list `A₀`, then it extends (together with
`A₀`) to a maximal consistent Henkin theory.

  Foundations.Logic.FO.Consistent (Γ₀.union (Foundations.Logic.FO.Theory.ofList A₀)) →
    Γ₀.Subset (Foundations.Logic.FO.henkinLimit hΓ₀ A₀) ∧
      (∀ (χ : Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula L), χ ∈ A₀ → Foundations.Logic.FO.henkinLimit hΓ₀ A₀ χ) ∧
        Foundations.Logic.FO.MaximalHenkin (Foundations.Logic.FO.henkinLimit hΓ₀ A₀)

**Cauchy product of exponential series**, finite form:
`Pₙ(a) Pₙ(b) = Pₙ(a + b) + Tₙ(a, b)` with `Pₙ(x) = Σ_{k<n} e x k`.
nodes.type:
∀ {α : Type} [inst : Lean.Grind.Field α] (e : α → Nat → α),
  (∀ (x : α), e x 0 = 1) →
    (∀ (x : α) (n : Nat), (↑n + 1) * e x (n + 1) = x * e x n) →
      (∀ (n : Nat), ↑n + 1 ≠ 0) →
        ∀ (a b : α) (N : Nat),
          Foundations.Numbers.gsum (e a) N * Foundations.Numbers.gsum (e b) N =
            Foundations.Numbers.gsum (e (a + b)) N +
              Foundations.Numbers.gsum (fun i => e a i * Foundations.Numbers.gsum (fun k => e b (N - i + k)) i) N

nodes.name: Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.recursion_theorem_set
nodes.doc:
**Recursion theorem, set-function form.** If `G` is a function from `A` to `A`
(a set of pairs) and `a ∈ A`, there is exactly one function `F` from `ω` to `A`
with `F(∅) = a` and `F(succ n) = G(F(n))`.
nodes.type:
∀ {A a G : Foundations.Sets.ZFSet},
  a ∈ A →
    G.IsFunction A A →
      ∃ F,
        F.IsFunction ω A ∧
          F.app ∅ = a ∧
            (∀ (n : Foundations.Sets.ZFSet), n ∈ ω → F.app n.succ = G.app (F.app n)) ∧
              ∀ (F' : Foundations.Sets.ZFSet),
                F'.IsFunction ω A →
                  F'.app ∅ = a → (∀ (n : Foundations.Sets.ZFSet), n ∈ ω → F'.app n.succ = G.app (F'.app n)) → F' = F

nodes.name: Foundations.Types.SystemF.fundamental
nodes.doc:

candidates, every substitution `σ` of reducible terms for the term variables, and
every substitution `τ` of types for the type variables, `t` (substituted) belongs

      (τ : Nat → Foundations.Types.SystemF.Ty),
      (∀ (n : Nat) (B : Foundations.Types.SystemF.Ty), Γ[n]? = some B → Foundations.Types.SystemF.RED ρ B (σ n)) →
        Foundations.Types.SystemF.RED ρ A
          (Foundations.Types.SystemF.Term.subst σ (Foundations.Types.SystemF.Term.tySubst τ t))

element: some `m` such that `r m x` implies `x = m`.

        (∀ (c : α → Prop), Foundations.Sets.Zorn.IsChain r c → ∃ u, ∀ (x : α), c x → r x u) →
          ∃ m, ∀ (x : α), r m x → x = m

function on judgements, there is a code which on input `a` finds a valid tree whose
root has key `a` (and diverges if there is none).
nodes.type:
∀ (step : Nat → Nat → Nat → Bool),
  (Foundations.Logic.Computability.CompB fun n =>
      step (Foundations.Logic.Computability.fst n)
        (Foundations.Logic.Computability.fst (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd n))
        (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd n))) →
    ∀ {key : Nat → Nat},
      Foundations.Logic.Computability.Comp key →
        ∃ c,
          (∀ (a t : Nat),
              Foundations.Logic.Computability.Eval c [a] t →
                Foundations.Logic.Computability.tvalid step t = 1 ∧ key (Foundations.Logic.Computability.troot t) = a) ∧
            ∀ (a : Nat),
              (∃ t,
                  Foundations.Logic.Computability.tvalid step t = 1 ∧
                    key (Foundations.Logic.Computability.troot t) = a) →
                ∃ t, Foundations.Logic.Computability.Eval c [a] t

  (∀ (us : Fin n → Foundations.Logic.FO.Term L) (k : Fin n),
      ∃ χ, ∀ (w : Foundations.Logic.FO.Term L), χ.inst w = Φ fun i => if i = k then w else us i) →
    ∀ {ts ts' : Fin n → Foundations.Logic.FO.Term L},
      (∀ (i : Fin n), Γ ⊢₁ Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula.eq (ts i) (ts' i)) → Γ ⊢₁ Φ ts → Γ ⊢₁ Φ ts'

nodes.name: Foundations.Algebra.secondIsoTheorem
nodes.doc:
**Second isomorphism theorem** (the "diamond" isomorphism). For a subgroup `H` and a
normal subgroup `N` of `G`, `H ⧸ (H ∩ N) ≃* HN ⧸ N`. Here `H ∩ N` and `N` are viewed as
(normal) subgroups of `H` and of `HN` respectively, via preimages under the inclusions.
nodes.type:
{G : Type u} →
  [inst : Foundations.Algebra.Group G] →
    (H N : Foundations.Algebra.Subgroup G) →
      [hN : N.Normal] →
        Foundations.Algebra.Iso
          (Foundations.Algebra.QuotientGroup (Foundations.Algebra.Subgroup.comap (Foundations.Algebra.Hom.subtype H) N))
          (Foundations.Algebra.QuotientGroup
            (Foundations.Algebra.Subgroup.comap (Foundations.Algebra.Hom.subtype (H.prodNormal N)) N))

nodes.name: Foundations.Geometry.rat_plane_axioms
nodes.doc:
**The rational plane satisfies the field-independent Tarski axioms**: (A1)–(A3),
(A5)–(A10) hold in `ℚ²` (they hold over every ordered field). Together with the two
failures above, this locates exactly where the real numbers are needed.
nodes.type:
(∀ (a b : Foundations.Geometry.Pt Foundations.Numbers.Q), a.Cong b b a) ∧
  (∀ (a b c : Foundations.Geometry.Pt Foundations.Numbers.Q), a.Cong b c c → a = b) ∧
    (∀ (a b : Foundations.Geometry.Pt Foundations.Numbers.Q), a.Bet b a → a = b) ∧
      (∀ (a b c p q : Foundations.Geometry.Pt Foundations.Numbers.Q),
          a.Bet p c → b.Bet q c → ∃ x, p.Bet x b ∧ q.Bet x a) ∧
        (∃ a b c, ¬a.Bet b c ∧ ¬b.Bet c a ∧ ¬c.Bet a b) ∧
          ∀ (a b c d t : Foundations.Geometry.Pt Foundations.Numbers.Q),
            a.Bet d t → b.Bet d c → a ≠ d → ∃ x y, a.Bet b x ∧ a.Bet c y ∧ x.Bet t y

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.R.rolle
nodes.doc:
**Rolle's theorem.** If `f` is continuous on `[a, b]`, differentiable on `(a, b)`, and
`f a = f b`, then `f' c = 0` at some `c` strictly between `a` and `b`.
nodes.type:
∀ {f f' : Foundations.Numbers.R → Foundations.Numbers.R} {a b : Foundations.Numbers.R},
  a < b →
    (∀ (x : Foundations.Numbers.R), a ≤ x → x ≤ b → Foundations.Numbers.R.ContinuousAt f x) →
      (∀ (x : Foundations.Numbers.R), a < x → x < b → Foundations.Numbers.R.HasDerivAt f (f' x) x) →
        f a = f b → ∃ c, a < c ∧ c < b ∧ f' c = 0

nodes.name: Foundations.Algebra.MulAction.orbit_smul

  Foundations.Algebra.MulAction.orbit G x y → ∀ (g : G), Foundations.Algebra.MulAction.orbit G x (g • y)

nodes.name: Foundations.Geometry.euclid_I_1
nodes.doc:
**Euclid, Elements I.1.** In the real plane, on every segment `ab` there is an
equilateral triangle `abc` (non-degenerate when `a ≠ b`). The proof needs `√3`,
supplied by the existence of square roots in `ℝ` — the continuity Euclid assumed.
nodes.type:
∀ (a b : Foundations.Geometry.Pt Foundations.Numbers.R),
  ∃ c, a.Cong b a c ∧ a.Cong b b c ∧ (a ≠ b → ¬a.Bet c b ∧ ¬c.Bet a b ∧ ¬a.Bet b c)

nodes.name: Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.cantor
nodes.doc:
**Cantor's theorem for sets.** For every set `x` and every operation `f` on
sets, `f` does not map the members of `x` onto the subsets of `x`: some subset
of `x` (namely `{z ∈ x | z ∉ f z}`) is not of the form `f z` with `z ∈ x`.
nodes.type:
∀ (x : Foundations.Sets.ZFSet) (f : Foundations.Sets.ZFSet → Foundations.Sets.ZFSet),
  ¬∀ (y : Foundations.Sets.ZFSet), y ∈ x.powerset → ∃ z, z ∈ x ∧ f z = y

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.Q.ordered_field
nodes.doc:
**`Q` is an ordered field (summary).** The field laws hold, and `≤` is a linear order
compatible with addition and with multiplication by positive elements.
nodes.type:
(∀ (x y z : Foundations.Numbers.Q), x + y + z = x + (y + z)) ∧
  (∀ (x y : Foundations.Numbers.Q), x + y = y + x) ∧
    (∀ (x : Foundations.Numbers.Q), x + 0 = x) ∧
      (∀ (x : Foundations.Numbers.Q), -x + x = 0) ∧
        (∀ (x y z : Foundations.Numbers.Q), x * y * z = x * (y * z)) ∧
          (∀ (x y : Foundations.Numbers.Q), x * y = y * x) ∧
            (∀ (x : Foundations.Numbers.Q), x * 1 = x) ∧
              (∀ (x y z : Foundations.Numbers.Q), x * (y + z) = x * y + x * z) ∧
                0 ≠ 1 ∧
                  (∀ (x : Foundations.Numbers.Q), x ≠ 0 → x * x⁻¹ = 1) ∧
                    (∀ (x y z : Foundations.Numbers.Q), x ≤ y → y ≤ z → x ≤ z) ∧
                      (∀ (x y : Foundations.Numbers.Q), x ≤ y → y ≤ x → x = y) ∧
                        (∀ (x y : Foundations.Numbers.Q), x ≤ y ∨ y ≤ x) ∧
                          (∀ (x y z : Foundations.Numbers.Q), x ≤ y → x + z ≤ y + z) ∧
                            ∀ (x y z : Foundations.Numbers.Q), x < y → 0 < z → z * x < z * y

nodes.name: Foundations.Logic.Computability.tvalid_iff
nodes.doc:
Unfolding validity: a tree is valid iff its root follows by a rule from the roots of
its subtrees, and all subtrees are smaller and valid.
nodes.type:
∀ (step : Nat → Nat → Nat → Bool) (t : Nat),
  Foundations.Logic.Computability.tvalid step t = 1 ↔
    step (Foundations.Logic.Computability.troot t)
          (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd (Foundations.Logic.Computability.fst t))
          (Foundations.Logic.Computability.fst (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd t)) =
        true ∧
      Foundations.Logic.Computability.llen
            (Foundations.Logic.Computability.fst (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd t)) =
          Foundations.Logic.Computability.llen
            (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd t)) ∧
        ∀ (i : Nat),
          i <
              Foundations.Logic.Computability.llen
                (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd t)) →
            Foundations.Logic.Computability.lnth
                  (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd t)) i <
                t ∧
              Foundations.Logic.Computability.tvalid step
                    (Foundations.Logic.Computability.lnth
                      (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd t)) i) =
                  1 ∧
                Foundations.Logic.Computability.troot
                    (Foundations.Logic.Computability.lnth
                      (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd t)) i) =
                  Foundations.Logic.Computability.lnth
                    (Foundations.Logic.Computability.fst (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd t)) i

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.R.ordered_field
nodes.doc:
**ℝ is an ordered field.** The field laws hold, every non-zero real has an inverse, and `≤`
is a linear order compatible with addition and with multiplication by positive reals.
nodes.type:
(∀ (x y z : Foundations.Numbers.R), x + y + z = x + (y + z)) ∧
  (∀ (x y : Foundations.Numbers.R), x + y = y + x) ∧
    (∀ (x : Foundations.Numbers.R), x + 0 = x) ∧
      (∀ (x : Foundations.Numbers.R), -x + x = 0) ∧
        (∀ (x y z : Foundations.Numbers.R), x * y * z = x * (y * z)) ∧
          (∀ (x y : Foundations.Numbers.R), x * y = y * x) ∧
            (∀ (x : Foundations.Numbers.R), x * 1 = x) ∧
              (∀ (x y z : Foundations.Numbers.R), x * (y + z) = x * y + x * z) ∧
                0 ≠ 1 ∧
                  (∀ (x : Foundations.Numbers.R), x ≠ 0 → x * x⁻¹ = 1) ∧
                    (∀ (x y z : Foundations.Numbers.R), x ≤ y → y ≤ z → x ≤ z) ∧
                      (∀ (x y : Foundations.Numbers.R), x ≤ y → y ≤ x → x = y) ∧
                        (∀ (x y : Foundations.Numbers.R), x ≤ y ∨ y ≤ x) ∧
                          (∀ (x y z : Foundations.Numbers.R), x ≤ y → x + z ≤ y + z) ∧
                            ∀ (x y z : Foundations.Numbers.R), x < y → 0 < z → z * x < z * y

**The binomial theorem for exponential terms.** If `e x 0 = 1` and
`(n + 1) · e x (n+1) = x · e x n` (as for `e x n = xⁿ/n!`), then
`Σ_{i ≤ n} e a i · e b (n − i) = e (a + b) n`.
nodes.type:
∀ {α : Type} [inst : Lean.Grind.Field α] (e : α → Nat → α),
  (∀ (x : α), e x 0 = 1) →
    (∀ (x : α) (n : Nat), (↑n + 1) * e x (n + 1) = x * e x n) →
      (∀ (n : Nat), ↑n + 1 ≠ 0) →
        ∀ (a b : α) (n : Nat), Foundations.Numbers.gsum (fun i => e a i * e b (n - i)) (n + 1) = e (a + b) n

nodes.name: Foundations.Geometry.Pt.stewart
nodes.doc:
Stewart's relation for a point `b = a + t (c − a)`:
`|bd|² = (1−t)|ad|² + t|cd|² − t(1−t)|ac|²`.
nodes.type:
∀ {K : Type} [inst : Lean.Grind.Field K] [inst_1 : LE K] [inst_2 : LT K] [inst_3 : Std.IsLinearOrder K]
  [Std.LawfulOrderLT K] [Lean.Grind.OrderedRing K] {a b c d : Foundations.Geometry.Pt K} {t : K},
  b.x - a.x = t * (c.x - a.x) →
    b.y - a.y = t * (c.y - a.y) → b.d2 d = (1 - t) * a.d2 d + t * c.d2 d - t * (1 - t) * a.d2 c

nodes.name: Foundations.Logic.Computability.incompleteness
nodes.doc:
**Abstract incompleteness theorem** (computational form of Gödel's first
incompleteness theorem; *abstract* — see the module docstring for exactly which
hypotheses remain to be discharged for a concrete system such as PA).

Let `Provable c x` mean "the formal system proves that code `c` does not halt on
input `x`". Suppose the system is
* **sound** for such statements: it proves only true ones; and
* **computably enumerable**: some code `q` halts on `(⌜c⌝, x)` exactly when
  `Provable c x`.

Then the system is **incomplete**: there is an explicit code `c` and input `x` such
that `c` does not halt on `x`, yet this is not provable. Namely `c = godelCode q` and
`x = ⌜c⌝` — the statement "I am not provable", in computational dress.
nodes.type:
∀ (Provable : Foundations.Logic.Computability.Code → Nat → Prop),
  (∀ (c : Foundations.Logic.Computability.Code) (x : Nat),
      Provable c x → ¬Foundations.Logic.Computability.Halts c [x]) →
    ∀ {q : Foundations.Logic.Computability.Code},
      (∀ (c : Foundations.Logic.Computability.Code) (x : Nat),
          Foundations.Logic.Computability.Halts q [Foundations.Logic.Computability.encode c, x] ↔ Provable c x) →
        ¬Foundations.Logic.Computability.Halts (Foundations.Logic.Computability.godelCode q)
              [Foundations.Logic.Computability.encode (Foundations.Logic.Computability.godelCode q)] ∧
          ¬Provable (Foundations.Logic.Computability.godelCode q)
              (Foundations.Logic.Computability.encode (Foundations.Logic.Computability.godelCode q))

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.Z.bridge_int
nodes.doc:
**Bridge theorem (ℤ).** The equivalence `Z ≃ Int` preserves `0`, `1`, addition, negation,
multiplication and order. So the integers built from pairs of naturals are the same structure as
Lean's `Int`, and we use `Int` from now on.
nodes.type:
Foundations.Numbers.Z.equivInt.toFun 0 = 0 ∧
  Foundations.Numbers.Z.equivInt.toFun 1 = 1 ∧
    (∀ (x y : Foundations.Numbers.Z),
        Foundations.Numbers.Z.equivInt.toFun (x + y) =
          Foundations.Numbers.Z.equivInt.toFun x + Foundations.Numbers.Z.equivInt.toFun y) ∧
      (∀ (x : Foundations.Numbers.Z),
          Foundations.Numbers.Z.equivInt.toFun (-x) = -Foundations.Numbers.Z.equivInt.toFun x) ∧
        (∀ (x y : Foundations.Numbers.Z),
            Foundations.Numbers.Z.equivInt.toFun (x * y) =
              Foundations.Numbers.Z.equivInt.toFun x * Foundations.Numbers.Z.equivInt.toFun y) ∧
          ∀ (x y : Foundations.Numbers.Z),
            x ≤ y ↔ Foundations.Numbers.Z.equivInt.toFun x ≤ Foundations.Numbers.Z.equivInt.toFun y

nodes.name: Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.recursion_theorem
nodes.doc:
**Dedekind's recursion theorem.** Let `a ∈ A` and let `g` map `A` into `A`.
Then there is exactly one function `F` from `ω` to `A` (a set of pairs) with
`F(∅) = a` and `F(succ n) = g(F(n))` for all `n ∈ ω`.
nodes.type:
∀ {A a : Foundations.Sets.ZFSet},
  a ∈ A →
    ∀ (g : Foundations.Sets.ZFSet → Foundations.Sets.ZFSet),
      (∀ (x : Foundations.Sets.ZFSet), x ∈ A → g x ∈ A) →
        ∃ F,
          F.IsFunction ω A ∧
            F.app ∅ = a ∧
              (∀ (n : Foundations.Sets.ZFSet), n ∈ ω → F.app n.succ = g (F.app n)) ∧
                ∀ (G : Foundations.Sets.ZFSet),
                  G.IsFunction ω A →
                    G.app ∅ = a → (∀ (n : Foundations.Sets.ZFSet), n ∈ ω → G.app n.succ = g (G.app n)) → G = F

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.N.bridge_nat
nodes.doc:
**Bridge theorem (ℕ).** The equivalence `N ≃ Nat` sends `0` to `0`, successor to `+1`,
and preserves addition, multiplication and order. Hence the home-made natural numbers and Lean's
`Nat` are the same structure, and we may use `Nat` from now on.
nodes.type:
Foundations.Numbers.N.equivNat.toFun Foundations.Numbers.N.zero = 0 ∧
  (∀ (n : Foundations.Numbers.N),
      Foundations.Numbers.N.equivNat.toFun n.succ = Foundations.Numbers.N.equivNat.toFun n + 1) ∧
    (∀ (a b : Foundations.Numbers.N),
        Foundations.Numbers.N.equivNat.toFun (a + b) =
          Foundations.Numbers.N.equivNat.toFun a + Foundations.Numbers.N.equivNat.toFun b) ∧
      (∀ (a b : Foundations.Numbers.N),
          Foundations.Numbers.N.equivNat.toFun (a * b) =
            Foundations.Numbers.N.equivNat.toFun a * Foundations.Numbers.N.equivNat.toFun b) ∧
        ∀ (a b : Foundations.Numbers.N),
          a ≤ b ↔ Foundations.Numbers.N.equivNat.toFun a ≤ Foundations.Numbers.N.equivNat.toFun b

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.R.abs_rsum_sub_rsum_le
nodes.doc:
**Comparison lemma.** If `|f s − f s'| ≤ ε` whenever `s, s' ∈ [A, B]` are within `2δ`, then
the Riemann sums over any two `δ`-fine partitions of `[a, b]` differ by at most `ε (b − a)`.
Proof: walk along both partitions simultaneously, each time cutting off the shorter of the two
first pieces.
nodes.type:
∀ {f : Foundations.Numbers.R → Foundations.Numbers.R} {A B δ ε : Foundations.Numbers.R},
  (∀ (s s' : Foundations.Numbers.R),
      A ≤ s →
        s ≤ B →
          A ≤ s' → s' ≤ B → Foundations.Numbers.OF.abs (s - s') < 2 * δ → Foundations.Numbers.OF.abs (f s - f s') ≤ ε) →
    ∀ (n : Nat) (a b : Foundations.Numbers.R) (P Q : List (Foundations.Numbers.R × Foundations.Numbers.R)),
      P.length + Q.length ≤ n →
        A.Fine B δ a P b →
          A.Fine B δ a Q b →
            Foundations.Numbers.OF.abs (Foundations.Numbers.R.rsum f a P - Foundations.Numbers.R.rsum f a Q) ≤
              ε * (b - a)

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.Arith.gcd

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.R.exists_mvt_point
nodes.doc:
On each piece `[a, x]` the increment of `F` is a value of `F'` times the length (mean value
theorem, also for degenerate pieces).
nodes.type:
∀ {F f : Foundations.Numbers.R → Foundations.Numbers.R} {a x : Foundations.Numbers.R},

    (∀ (t : Foundations.Numbers.R), a ≤ t → t ≤ x → Foundations.Numbers.R.HasDerivAt F (f t) t) →
      ∃ c, a ≤ c ∧ c ≤ x ∧ F x - F a = f c * (x - a)

nodes.name: Foundations.Algebra.Group
nodes.doc:
**Group.** A group is a type `G` with a multiplication, a distinguished element `1`
and an inversion `a ↦ a⁻¹`, such that multiplication is associative, `1` is a left
identity and `a⁻¹` is a left inverse of `a`. (The right-handed versions are theorems,

nodes.name: Foundations.Logic.FO.qjs
nodes.doc: The coded list of premises.

nodes.type:

nodes.name: Foundations.Algebra.MulAction.smul_eq_smul_iff
nodes.doc:
`g • x = h • x` exactly when `h⁻¹ * g` stabilises `x`: the elements sending `x` to a given
point form a left coset of the stabiliser.
nodes.type:
∀ {G : Type u} [inst : Foundations.Algebra.Group G] {X : Type v} [inst_1 : Foundations.Algebra.MulAction G X] (g h : G)
  (x : X), g • x = h • x ↔ Foundations.Algebra.leftCoset h (Foundations.Algebra.MulAction.stabilizer G x) g

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.R.abs_neg

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.C.exists_min_on_square
nodes.doc:
**Two-dimensional extreme value theorem.** A non-negative function `g : ℂ → ℝ`, continuous
everywhere, attains its minimum on every closed square `|re z|, |im z| ≤ ρ`.
nodes.type:
∀ {g : Foundations.Numbers.C → Foundations.Numbers.R} {ρ : Foundations.Numbers.R},
  0 ≤ ρ →
    (∀ (z : Foundations.Numbers.C), 0 ≤ g z) →
      (∀ (z₀ : Foundations.Numbers.C) (ε : Foundations.Numbers.R),
          0 < ε →
            ∃ δ,
              0 < δ ∧ ∀ (z : Foundations.Numbers.C), (z - z₀).cabs < δ → Foundations.Numbers.OF.abs (g z - g z₀) < ε) →
        ∃ zs,
          Foundations.Numbers.C.InSq ρ zs ∧ ∀ (z : Foundations.Numbers.C), Foundations.Numbers.C.InSq ρ z → g zs ≤ g z

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.C.zero_ne_one

nodes.name: Foundations.Types.STLC.case_red
nodes.doc:

are reducible under every reducible substitution.

  Foundations.Types.STLC.RED (A.sum B) t →
    (∀ (a : Foundations.Types.STLC.Term),

          Foundations.Types.STLC.RED B b → Foundations.Types.STLC.RED C (Foundations.Types.STLC.inst u₂ b)) →
        Foundations.Types.STLC.RED C (t.case u₁ u₂)

nodes.name: Foundations.Algebra.cayley_finite

**Cayley's theorem for finite groups.** A finite group of order `n` embeds into the
symmetric group `Sₙ = Perm (Fin n)`: there is an injective homomorphism
`G →* Perm (Fin (card G))`.
nodes.type:
∀ {G : Type u} [inst : Foundations.Algebra.Group G] [inst_1 : Foundations.Algebra.FiniteType G],
  ∃ f, ∀ (a b : G), f.toFun a = f.toFun b → a = b

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.Categoricity.map_neg
nodes.doc: An additive map preserves negation.
nodes.type:
∀ {F : Type} [inst : Lean.Grind.Field F] [inst_1 : LE F] [inst_2 : LT F] [inst_3 : Std.IsLinearOrder F]
  [Std.LawfulOrderLT F] [Lean.Grind.OrderedRing F] {G : Type} [inst_6 : Lean.Grind.Field G] [inst_7 : LE G]
  [inst_8 : LT G] [inst_9 : Std.IsLinearOrder G] [Std.LawfulOrderLT G] [Lean.Grind.OrderedRing G] {ψ : F → G},
  (∀ (x y : F), ψ (x + y) = ψ x + ψ y) → ∀ (x : F), ψ (-x) = -ψ x

nodes.name: Foundations.Algebra.MulAction.count_smul_mem
nodes.doc:
Counting by fibres: for any part `Q` of the orbit of `x`, the number of `g` with
`g • x ∈ Q` is `|Q| · |Stab x|`. Proved by removing one point of `Q` at a time.
nodes.type:
∀ {G : Type u} [inst : Foundations.Algebra.Group G] {X : Type v} [inst_1 : Foundations.Algebra.MulAction G X]
  [inst_2 : Foundations.Algebra.FiniteType G] [inst_3 : Foundations.Algebra.FiniteType X] (x : X) (n : Nat)
  (Q : X → Prop),
  Foundations.Algebra.FiniteType.count Q = n →
    (∀ (y : X), Q y → Foundations.Algebra.MulAction.orbit G x y) →
      (Foundations.Algebra.FiniteType.count fun g => Q (g • x)) =
        n * Foundations.Algebra.FiniteType.count fun x_1 => x_1 ∈ Foundations.Algebra.MulAction.stabilizer G x

        (∀ (φ ψ : Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula Foundations.Logic.FO.Arith), P φ → P ψ → P (φ.conj ψ)) →
          (∀ (φ ψ : Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula Foundations.Logic.FO.Arith), P φ → P ψ → P (φ.disj ψ)) →

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.Z.comm_ring

**ℤ is a commutative ring.** The integers satisfy all the axioms of a commutative ring
with `0 ≠ 1`.

(∀ (x y z : Foundations.Numbers.Z), x + y + z = x + (y + z)) ∧
  (∀ (x y : Foundations.Numbers.Z), x + y = y + x) ∧
    (∀ (x : Foundations.Numbers.Z), x + 0 = x) ∧
      (∀ (x : Foundations.Numbers.Z), -x + x = 0) ∧
        (∀ (x y z : Foundations.Numbers.Z), x * y * z = x * (y * z)) ∧
          (∀ (x y : Foundations.Numbers.Z), x * y = y * x) ∧
            (∀ (x : Foundations.Numbers.Z), x * 1 = x) ∧
              (∀ (x y z : Foundations.Numbers.Z), x * (y + z) = x * y + x * z) ∧ 0 ≠ 1

nodes.name: Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.arith_bridge

multiplication of Lean's natural numbers correspond exactly to `∅`, `succ`, `+ω`
and `*ω`, which were defined purely set-theoretically by the recursion theorem.
nodes.type:
Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn 0 = ∅ ∧
  (∀ (n : Nat), Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn (n + 1) = (Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn n).succ) ∧
    (∀ (m n : Nat), Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn (m + n) = Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn m +ω Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn n) ∧
      ∀ (m n : Nat), Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn (m * n) = Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn m *ω Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn n

nodes.name: Foundations.Categories.lawvere_fixed_point
nodes.doc:
**Lawvere's fixed-point theorem.** Let `A × A` be a product (projections `p₁, p₂`)
and `φ : A × A ⟶ B` be point-surjective with respect to `T`-points: for every
`g : A ⟶ B` there is `a : T ⟶ A` with `φ ∘ ⟨a, x⟩ = g ∘ x` for all `x : T ⟶ A`. Then every
`t : B ⟶ B` has a fixed `T`-point `b : T ⟶ B`, `b ≫ t = b`.
nodes.type:
∀ {C : Type u} [inst : Foundations.Categories.Category C] {A B AA T : C}
  {p₁ p₂ : Foundations.Categories.Category.Hom AA A} (hP : Foundations.Categories.IsProduct A A AA p₁ p₂)
  (φ : Foundations.Categories.Category.Hom AA B),
  (∀ (g : Foundations.Categories.Category.Hom A B),
      ∃ a,
        ∀ (x : Foundations.Categories.Category.Hom T A),
          Foundations.Categories.Category.comp (hP.lift a x) φ = Foundations.Categories.Category.comp x g) →
    ∀ (t : Foundations.Categories.Category.Hom B B), ∃ b, Foundations.Categories.Category.comp b t = b

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.Bisect.spec
nodes.doc:
The bisection invariant: `P` fails at each left end, holds at each right end, the intervals
are ordered, and the `n`-th interval has length `(u − l)/2ⁿ`.
nodes.type:
∀ {P : Foundations.Numbers.Q → Prop} {l u : Foundations.Numbers.Q},
  ¬P l →
    P u →
      l ≤ u →
        ∀ (n : Nat),
          ¬P (Foundations.Numbers.Bisect.lo P l u n) ∧
            P (Foundations.Numbers.Bisect.hi P l u n) ∧
              Foundations.Numbers.Bisect.lo P l u n ≤ Foundations.Numbers.Bisect.hi P l u n ∧
                (Foundations.Numbers.Bisect.hi P l u n - Foundations.Numbers.Bisect.lo P l u n) * 2 ^ n = u - l

nodes.name: Foundations.Algebra.PolyList.mul_top
nodes.doc:
**Top coefficients multiply** (list version). If `p` vanishes from index `s + 1` on and
`q` from index `t + 1` on, then the coefficient of `p·q` at `s + t` is `pₛ·qₜ`, and `p·q`
vanishes from index `s + t + 1` on.
nodes.type:
∀ {R : Type u} [inst : Foundations.Algebra.CommRing R] (q : List R) (t : Nat),
  (∀ (n : Nat), t + 1 ≤ n → Foundations.Algebra.PolyList.coeff q n = 0) →
    ∀ (p : List R) (s : Nat),
      (∀ (n : Nat), s + 1 ≤ n → Foundations.Algebra.PolyList.coeff p n = 0) →
        Foundations.Algebra.PolyList.coeff (Foundations.Algebra.PolyList.mul p q) (s + t) =
            Foundations.Algebra.PolyList.coeff p s * Foundations.Algebra.PolyList.coeff q t ∧
          ∀ (n : Nat), s + t + 1 ≤ n → Foundations.Algebra.PolyList.coeff (Foundations.Algebra.PolyList.mul p q) n = 0

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.C.dalembert

then `|b₀ + wᵏ (b + w r(w))| < |b₀|` for some `w`: a polynomial does not have a local minimum of
its modulus at a non-zero value.
nodes.type:
∀ {b₀ b : Foundations.Numbers.C},
  b₀ ≠ 0 →
    b ≠ 0 →
      ∀ {k : Nat},
        1 ≤ k →
          ∀ (r : Foundations.Numbers.C → Foundations.Numbers.C) {M : Foundations.Numbers.R},
            (∀ (w : Foundations.Numbers.C), w.cabs ≤ 1 → (r w).cabs ≤ M) →
              ∃ w, (b₀ + w ^ k * (b + w * r w)).cabs < b₀.cabs

nodes.name: Foundations.Logic.FO.lowenheim_skolem
nodes.doc:
**Downward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem.** If a theory in a countable language is
satisfied in any structure at all (with domain in `Type`, under some environment),
then it is satisfied in a countable one: a structure admitting a surjection from `ℕ`
onto its domain.
nodes.type:
∀ {L : Foundations.Logic.FO.Signature} [L.Countable] {Γ : Foundations.Logic.FO.Theory L}

  (∀ (ψ : Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula L), Γ ψ → Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula.Sat M e ψ) →
    ∃ N e',
      (∀ (ψ : Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula L), Γ ψ → Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula.Sat N e' ψ) ∧
        ∃ f, ∀ (x : N.Dom), ∃ n, f n = x

would apply to this "theory of true arithmetic" in place of PA.

    ∀ (φ : Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula Foundations.Logic.FO.Arith),
      Foundations.Logic.Computability.Halts c [Foundations.Logic.FO.fcode φ] ↔
        ∀ (e : Nat → Nat), Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula.Sat Foundations.Logic.FO.stdModel e φ

  (Foundations.Algebra.tprod fun i => x (i + Fin.ofNat (m + 1) 1)) = (x 0)⁻¹ * Foundations.Algebra.tprod x * x 0

nodes.name: Foundations.Logic.Computability.rice
nodes.doc:
**Rice's theorem.** Let `P` be a property of codes that depends only on the
(unary) partial function they compute, and is non-trivial (some code has it, some
does not). Then `P` is undecidable: no code, total on Gödel numbers, outputs `0`
exactly on the numbers of codes lacking `P`.
nodes.type:
∀ (P : Foundations.Logic.Computability.Code → Prop),
  (∀ (c c' : Foundations.Logic.Computability.Code),
      (∀ (x n : Nat), Foundations.Logic.Computability.Eval c [x] n ↔ Foundations.Logic.Computability.Eval c' [x] n) →
        (P c ↔ P c')) →
    ∀ {a b : Foundations.Logic.Computability.Code},
      P a →
        ¬P b →
          ¬∃ r,
              ∀ (c : Foundations.Logic.Computability.Code),
                Foundations.Logic.Computability.Halts r [Foundations.Logic.Computability.encode c] ∧
                  (Foundations.Logic.Computability.Eval r [Foundations.Logic.Computability.encode c] 0 ↔ ¬P c)

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.R.poly_reflect

  Foundations.Numbers.R.Vanish e d →
    ∀ (P : Foundations.Numbers.R),
      (∀ (y : Foundations.Numbers.R), Foundations.Numbers.R.poly e d (P - y) = Foundations.Numbers.R.poly e d y) →
        ∀ (m : Nat) (y : Foundations.Numbers.R),
          Foundations.Numbers.R.poly (Foundations.Numbers.R.iterD m e) d (P - y) =
            (-1) ^ m * Foundations.Numbers.R.poly (Foundations.Numbers.R.iterD m e) d y

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.R.mean_value
nodes.doc:
**Mean value theorem** (Lagrange). If `f` is continuous on `[a, b]` and differentiable on
`(a, b)`, then the chord slope is attained as a derivative: `f b − f a = f' c · (b − a)` for some
`c` strictly between `a` and `b`.
nodes.type:
∀ {f f' : Foundations.Numbers.R → Foundations.Numbers.R} {a b : Foundations.Numbers.R},
  a < b →
    (∀ (x : Foundations.Numbers.R), a ≤ x → x ≤ b → Foundations.Numbers.R.ContinuousAt f x) →
      (∀ (x : Foundations.Numbers.R), a < x → x < b → Foundations.Numbers.R.HasDerivAt f (f' x) x) →
        ∃ c, a < c ∧ c < b ∧ f b - f a = f' c * (b - a)

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.R.uniform_continuous
nodes.doc:
**Heine–Cantor theorem.** A function continuous at every point of `[a, b]` is *uniformly*
continuous on `[a, b]`: for every `ε > 0` one `δ > 0` works for all pairs of points.
nodes.type:
∀ {f : Foundations.Numbers.R → Foundations.Numbers.R} {a b : Foundations.Numbers.R},
  (∀ (x : Foundations.Numbers.R), a ≤ x → x ≤ b → Foundations.Numbers.R.ContinuousAt f x) →
    ∀ {ε : Foundations.Numbers.R},
      0 < ε →
        ∃ δ,
          0 < δ ∧
            ∀ (s t : Foundations.Numbers.R),
              a ≤ s →
                s ≤ b →
                  a ≤ t → t ≤ b → Foundations.Numbers.OF.abs (s - t) < δ → Foundations.Numbers.OF.abs (f s - f t) < ε

nodes.name: Foundations.Algebra.pGroup_center
nodes.doc:
**Non-trivial `p`-groups have non-trivial centre.** If `|G| = p ^ k` with `p` prime and
`k ≥ 1`, then `p` divides the order of the centre; in particular the centre contains an
element other than `1`. (This is the class equation `|G| = |Z(G)| + Σ [G : C(xᵢ)]`, read
modulo `p`.)
nodes.type:
∀ {G : Type u} [inst : Foundations.Algebra.Group G] [inst_1 : Foundations.Algebra.FiniteType G] {p k : Nat},
  Foundations.Algebra.IsPrime p →
    1 ≤ k →
      Foundations.Algebra.FiniteType.card G = p ^ k →
        p ∣ Foundations.Algebra.FiniteType.card { x // x ∈ Foundations.Algebra.center G }

nodes.name: Foundations.Algebra.exists_subgroup_card_pow_succ

**One rung of the ladder.** If `H` has order `p ^ j` and `p ^ (j+1)` divides `|G|`, then

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.C.fta
nodes.doc:
**The fundamental theorem of algebra.** Every non-constant polynomial with complex
coefficients has a complex root: if some coefficient of `t` is non-zero, the polynomial
`c₀ + z · t(z)` (coefficient list `c₀ :: t`) vanishes somewhere.
nodes.type:

nodes.name: Foundations.Logic.Valuation.exists_row

there is a row of the truth table for `l` agreeing with `v` on every atom of `l`.

  ∃ w, w ∈ Foundations.Logic.Valuation.rows l ∧ ∀ (a : Nat), a ∈ l → w a = v a

interpretations of the function and relation symbols. (The domain is not required

nodes.name: Foundations.Logic.FO.extendH_decides

Each processed formula was either accepted with its witnesses, or rejected
because it is inconsistent with part of the result.
nodes.type:
∀ {L : Foundations.Logic.FO.Signature} {Γ₀ : Foundations.Logic.FO.Theory L} (hΓ₀ : Foundations.Logic.FO.FreshSupply Γ₀)
  (l A : List (Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula L)) (ψ : Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula L),
  ψ ∈ l →
    ∃ A',
      (∀ (χ : Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula L), χ ∈ A' → χ ∈ Foundations.Logic.FO.extendH hΓ₀ A l) ∧
        ((∀ (χ : Foundations.Logic.FO.Formula L),
            χ ∈ Foundations.Logic.FO.henkinAdd hΓ₀ A' ψ → χ ∈ Foundations.Logic.FO.extendH hΓ₀ A l) ∨
          ¬Foundations.Logic.FO.Consistent (Γ₀.union (Foundations.Logic.FO.Theory.ofList (ψ :: A'))))

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.nat_to_real_embedding
nodes.doc:
**The chain ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ.** The composite embedding of the natural numbers into the reals
is injective and preserves addition and multiplication.
nodes.type:
have ι := fun n => Foundations.Numbers.R.ofQ (Foundations.Numbers.zToQ (Foundations.Numbers.natToZ n));
(∀ (a b : Nat), ι (a + b) = ι a + ι b) ∧ (∀ (a b : Nat), ι (a * b) = ι a * ι b) ∧ ∀ (a b : Nat), ι a = ι b → a = b

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.R.ftc2
nodes.doc:
**Fundamental theorem of calculus, part II.** If `F' = f` on `[a, b]` and `f` has integral
`I` over `[a, b]`, then `I = F b − F a`.
nodes.type:
∀ {F f : Foundations.Numbers.R → Foundations.Numbers.R} {a b I : Foundations.Numbers.R},
  a ≤ b →
    (∀ (t : Foundations.Numbers.R), a ≤ t → t ≤ b → Foundations.Numbers.R.HasDerivAt F (f t) t) →
      Foundations.Numbers.R.HasIntegral f a b I → I = F b - F a

nodes.name: Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.exists_wellOrdered_not_le

∀ (α : Type),
  ∃ H lt,
    (∀ (x y z : H), lt x y → lt y z → lt x z) ∧
      (∀ (x y : H), lt x y ∨ x = y ∨ lt y x) ∧ WellFounded lt ∧ ¬Foundations.Sets.CardLE H α

`x ≡ b (mod n)`.

  m.Coprime n →
    ∀ (a b : Nat),
      a < m → b < n → ∃ x, x < m * n ∧ x % m = a ∧ x % n = b ∧ ∀ (y : Nat), y < m * n → y % m = a → y % n = b → y = x

nodes.name: Foundations.Algebra.MulAction.count_fixed_mod_of_invariant
nodes.doc:
**The fixed-point congruence (class equation modulo `p`).** If a group of order `p ^ k`
(with `p` prime) acts on a finite set `X`, then the number of fixed points is congruent to
`|X|` modulo `p`. More generally this holds for every invariant subset `P` of `X`. Proof:
peel off one non-trivial orbit at a time; each has size a multiple of `p`.
nodes.type:
∀ {G : Type u} [inst : Foundations.Algebra.Group G] {X : Type v} [inst_1 : Foundations.Algebra.MulAction G X]
  [inst_2 : Foundations.Algebra.FiniteType G] [inst_3 : Foundations.Algebra.FiniteType X] {p k : Nat},
  Foundations.Algebra.IsPrime p →
    Foundations.Algebra.FiniteType.card G = p ^ k →
      ∀ (n : Nat) (P : X → Prop),
        Foundations.Algebra.FiniteType.count P = n →
          (∀ (g : G) (y : X), P y → P (g • y)) →
            (Foundations.Algebra.FiniteType.count fun y => P y ∧ Foundations.Algebra.MulAction.IsFixed G y) % p = n % p

false. (Here cut elimination and truth tables work together.)

      (Foundations.Types.STLC.Ty.arr

        (Foundations.Types.STLC.Ty.atom k))

nodes.name: Foundations.Algebra.fundamental_theorem_of_arithmetic

of irreducible integers, and any two such factorisations agree up to order and signs.

∀ (a : Int),
  a ≠ 0 →
    ¬Foundations.Algebra.IsUnit a →
      (∃ L, (∀ (p : Int), p ∈ L → Foundations.Algebra.Irreducible p) ∧ Foundations.Algebra.lprod L = a) ∧
        ∀ (L M : List Int),
          (∀ (p : Int), p ∈ L → Foundations.Algebra.Irreducible p) →
            (∀ (q : Int), q ∈ M → Foundations.Algebra.Irreducible q) →
              Foundations.Algebra.lprod L = a →
                Foundations.Algebra.lprod M = a →
                  ∀ (x : Int), Foundations.Algebra.countAssoc x L = Foundations.Algebra.countAssoc x M

  0 < ε →
    ∃ N,
      ∀ (n : Nat),
        N ≤ n →
          Foundations.Numbers.R.ofQ (a.seq n) - Foundations.Numbers.R.ofQ ε ≤ Foundations.Numbers.R.mk a ∧
            Foundations.Numbers.R.mk a ≤ Foundations.Numbers.R.ofQ (a.seq n) + Foundations.Numbers.R.ofQ ε

∀ {F : Type u} [inst : Foundations.Algebra.CommRing F],
  Foundations.Algebra.IsField F →
    ∀ (n : Nat) (p : Foundations.Algebra.Polynomial F),
      p.natDegree = n →
        p ≠ 0 →
          ¬Foundations.Algebra.IsUnit p →

nodes.name: Foundations.Logic.FO.eval_prec_iff_beta
nodes.doc: Primitive recursion, unfolded with a β-coded sequence of intermediate values.
nodes.type:
∀ (f g : Foundations.Logic.Computability.Code) (xs : List Nat) (m y : Nat),
  Foundations.Logic.Computability.Eval (f.prec g) (m :: xs) y ↔
    ∃ A B,
      Foundations.Logic.Computability.Eval f xs (Foundations.Logic.FO.gbeta A B 0) ∧
        (∀ (j : Nat),
            j < m →
              Foundations.Logic.Computability.Eval g (j :: Foundations.Logic.FO.gbeta A B j :: xs)
                (Foundations.Logic.FO.gbeta A B (j + 1))) ∧
          y = Foundations.Logic.FO.gbeta A B m

nodes.name: Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.omega_bridge
nodes.doc:
**Bridge theorem (ω ≅ ℕ).** The map `vn : Nat → ZFSet` sends `0` to `∅`
and `n + 1` to `succ (vn n)`, is injective, and its values are exactly the
members of `ω`; moreover it turns `<` into `∈` and `≤` into `⊆`. Hence `ω`
with `∅` and `succ` is an exact copy of Lean's natural numbers.
nodes.type:
Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn 0 = ∅ ∧
  (∀ (n : Nat), Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn (n + 1) = (Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn n).succ) ∧
    Function.Injective Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn ∧
      (∀ (x : Foundations.Sets.ZFSet), x ∈ ω ↔ ∃ n, Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn n = x) ∧
        (∀ (m n : Nat), m < n ↔ Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn m ∈ Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn n) ∧
          ∀ (m n : Nat), m ≤ n ↔ Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn m ⊆ Foundations.Sets.ZFSet.vn n

    ∀ (a : Nat),

            Foundations.Logic.Computability.pair
                (Foundations.Logic.Computability.fst (Foundations.Logic.Computability.troot t))
                (Foundations.Logic.Computability.fst
                  (Foundations.Logic.Computability.snd (Foundations.Logic.Computability.troot t))) =

nodes.name: Foundations.Numbers.CauSeq.abs_mul_sub_lt

`|y'| ≤ B` and the differences are below `ε/(A+B)`, the products differ by less than `ε`.
nodes.type:
∀ {x y x' y' A B ε : Foundations.Numbers.Q},
  0 < A →
    0 < B →
      0 < ε →
        x.abs ≤ A → y'.abs ≤ B → (y - y').abs < ε / (A + B) → (x - x').abs < ε / (A + B) → (x * y - x' * y').abs < ε

modules.doc:
# Pre-sets: Aczel's model of sets inside type theory

Lean's foundation is a *type theory*, not a set theory. To speak about sets in
the sense of Zermelo–Fraenkel (ZF), we build a model of ZF inside type theory,
following Peter Aczel's idea (1978).

The guiding picture is the *cumulative hierarchy*: a set is nothing but the
collection of its members, and those members are again sets. A **pre-set** makes
this picture literal: a pre-set is given by an *index type* `α` together with a
family `A : α → PSet` that lists the members, one for every index. Since the
members are again pre-sets, `PSet` is an inductive type — every pre-set is built
in well-founded stages, just like the cumulative hierarchy.

A pre-set is a *presentation* of a set, not yet the set itself: the same members
may be listed twice, or in a different order, or with different index types. Two
pre-sets should count as "the same set" exactly when every member of one has an
equal member in the other, and vice versa. This **extensional equivalence**
`PSet.Equiv` is defined by recursion and shown to be an equivalence relation. In
the next file (`ZFSet`) we pass to the quotient, which identifies equivalent
presentations: that quotient is our universe of sets.

*Universe bookkeeping.* Index types live in `Type` (universe 0), so `PSet` itself
lives one universe higher, in `Type 1`. This is the type-theoretic shadow of the
fact that the collection of all sets is not itself a set.

# ZF sets and the axioms of Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory

We now pass from *presentations* of sets to sets themselves. A `ZFSet` is an
equivalence class of pre-sets under extensional equivalence: two pre-sets that
have the same members are identified. In philosophical terms, the quotient is
what turns the intensional notion "a way of listing members" into the
extensional notion "a collection, individuated by its members alone".

Membership descends to the quotient because it respects equivalence (proved in
`PSet`). From then on we never look at presentations again, except in two
places:

* **The family principle** `mem_ofFamily`: for any index type `α : Type` and any
  family `f : α → ZFSet` there is a set whose members are exactly the values
  `f a`. Every set-forming operation of ZF — empty set, pairing, union, power set,
  separation, replacement, the infinite set — is obtained from this one
  principle by choosing a suitable index type. (Choosing representatives of the
  `f a` uses the axiom of choice of the ambient logic; this is harmless and
  keeps every construction a one-liner.)
* **∈-induction** `mem_induction`: since pre-sets are built in well-founded
  stages, so are sets; this is the axiom of foundation (regularity).

The axioms of ZF then become *theorems* about this model:
extensionality, empty set, pairing, union, power set, separation, replacement,
infinity and foundation. That the model satisfies them is what justifies
calling `ZFSet` "the universe of sets" in the rest of the project.

# The paradoxes: Russell and Cantor

Naive set theory, in Frege's form, held that every property determines a set:
the set of all things having it. Russell (1901) showed that this is
inconsistent. Consider the property "is not a member of itself". If there were
a set `R` of exactly the sets with that property, then `R ∈ R` would hold if and
only if `R ∉ R` — a contradiction.

ZF escapes by allowing only *separation*: a property may carve a subset out of
an already given set, but need not determine a set outright. Run through
separation, Russell's argument stops being a paradox and becomes a theorem:
**there is no set of all sets**. Our proof uses only separation, not foundation.

The underlying pattern is purely logical — *no barber shaves exactly those who
do not shave themselves* — and we isolate it first. The same diagonal pattern
gives **Cantor's theorem**: no set can be mapped onto the collection of its
subsets. We prove it both for Lean types (with subsets as predicates) and for
ZF sets (with the power set). Cantor's theorem is the source of the endless
hierarchy of infinite sizes; Russell found his paradox by applying Cantor's
argument to the "set of all sets".

# The von Neumann natural numbers and the set ω

What *is* the number 3? Frege answered: the class of all three-membered classes —
an answer Russell's paradox made untenable. Von Neumann (1923) proposed instead
to let each number be one particular, canonical set: the set of all smaller
numbers.

    0 = ∅,   1 = {0},   2 = {0, 1},   3 = {0, 1, 2},   …,   n + 1 = n ∪ {n}.

These sets `vn n` were defined in `ZFSet`, together with the set `ω` of all of
them, whose existence is the axiom of infinity. Here we show that `ω` behaves
exactly as the natural numbers should, by proving the **Peano axioms** for it:
zero is a number, every number has a successor, successors are injective, zero
is no successor, and induction holds.

Finally, the **bridge theorem** shows that `vn` is a one-to-one correspondence
between Lean's built-in natural numbers and the members of `ω`, sending zero to
`∅` and `n + 1` to the successor set; under it, `<` becomes `∈` and `≤` becomes
`⊆`. This is what licenses later parts of the project to use Lean's `Nat` as a
convenient stand-in for the set-theoretic numbers.


## Members of a von Neumann natural 

## The Peano axioms for ω 

## The bridge between `Nat` and ω

# Set algebra, ordered pairs and cartesian products

Sets are unordered: `{a, b} = {b, a}`. Yet mathematics constantly needs *ordered*
pairs — the point `(3, 5)` differs from `(5, 3)` — and with them relations and
functions. Kuratowski (1921) found a purely set-theoretic definition:

    ⟪a, b⟫ := {{a}, {a, b}}.

Nothing about this set "is" an order; what matters is only that it does the job
of one: `⟪a, b⟫ = ⟪c, d⟫` holds exactly when `a = c` and `b = d`. This is an early
and instructive example of the structuralist attitude that pervades the
foundations of mathematics — an object is characterised by its role, not by any
intrinsic nature.

We first add intersection and difference (both by separation), then prove the
characteristic property of Kuratowski pairs, and finally build the cartesian
product `x × y` by separating the pairs out of the power set of the power set of
`x ∪ y` — a nice illustration of how the ZF axioms bound where new sets can come
from.


## Intersection and difference 

## Singletons and unordered pairs 

## Kuratowski ordered pairs 

## Cartesian products

# The Schröder–Bernstein theorem

Cantor measured the size of a collection by one-to-one correspondence: two
collections have the same size when their members can be paired off exactly.
"`α` is at most as large as `β`" then means: `α` can be injected into `β`. For
this to be a genuine *order* of sizes, it must be antisymmetric: if each of two
collections is at most as large as the other, they must have the same size.
That is the content of the **Schröder–Bernstein theorem** (Cantor conjectured
it; Dedekind, Schröder and Bernstein proved it in the 1880s–90s).

Proof idea. Given injections `f : α → β` and `g : β → α`, follow the "ancestry"
of each point of `α`. Call a point *Cantor-type* (`InC`) if, tracing back along
`g` and `f`, one eventually reaches a point of `α` not hit by `g`. Inductively:
points outside the range of `g` are in `InC`, and if `a` is in `InC` so is
`g (f a)`. On `InC` we use `f`; elsewhere we use the inverse of `g`, which is
available because points outside `InC` are in the range of `g`. Classical logic
is used to decide membership in `InC`.

# Von Neumann ordinals and the Burali-Forti paradox

The natural numbers count *how many*; ordinals count *how far along* — they are
the measure of position in a well-ordered sequence, and they continue past every
natural number: `0, 1, 2, …, ω, ω + 1, …`. Von Neumann's insight is that, as with
the naturals, each ordinal can be taken to be the set of all smaller ordinals,
ordered by membership.

Formally, a set is **transitive** if every member of it is also a subset of it
(members of members are members), and an **ordinal** is a transitive set all of
whose members are transitive. (In the presence of foundation this simple
definition suffices: membership is then automatically well-founded.)

We show that every von Neumann natural and `ω` itself are ordinals, that the
members of an ordinal are ordinals, and that membership is a strict linear order
on ordinals — irreflexive, transitive and *trichotomous*: of two ordinals, one
is a member of the other or they are equal.

Finally, **Burali-Forti's paradox** (1897): there is no set of all ordinals.
Such a set would itself be an ordinal, hence a member of itself — which
foundation forbids. Like Russell's paradox, this marks the boundary between
the sets and the "too large" totalities, such as *all sets* or *all ordinals*,
that cannot be gathered into a set.

# Dedekind's recursion theorem

In *Was sind und was sollen die Zahlen?* (1888) Dedekind faced a question that
looks almost too innocent to ask: what entitles us to *define* a function on the
natural numbers by recursion — "`F(0) = a`, and `F(n + 1) = g(F(n))`"? Such a
clause only says how to get from one value to the next; that it determines a
single, completed function is a theorem, not a triviality. Dedekind proved it,
and this file reproduces his proof inside our model of ZF.

First we say what a *function* is, set-theoretically: a set `F` of Kuratowski
pairs inside a cartesian product `X × A` containing, for every `x ∈ X`, exactly
one pair `⟪x, y⟫`. We write `app F x` for that unique `y`.

The proof of the recursion theorem is Dedekind's own. Call a set `R` *closed*
if it contains `⟪∅, a⟫` and, together with any `⟪n, y⟫` with `n ∈ ω`, also
contains `⟪succ n, g y⟫`. Let `F` be the set of pairs in `ω × A` lying in *every*
closed set — the least closed relation. Then `F` is closed, and induction on `ω`
shows that it is a function: if `F` contained a second, "rogue" pair above some
`n`, removing it would leave a smaller closed set, contradicting minimality.
Uniqueness is another induction. Note that the proof uses only set-theoretic
means — no appeal to Lean's built-in natural numbers.


## Functions as sets of pairs 

## The least closed relation 

## The recursion theorem

# Arithmetic on ω

With the recursion theorem in hand, arithmetic can be *defined* inside set
theory, exactly as Dedekind and Peano taught: addition is iterated successor,
and multiplication is iterated addition.

    m + 0 = m,      m + succ n = succ (m + n);
    m · 0 = 0,      m · succ n = m · n + m.

For each fixed `m ∈ ω`, the recursion theorem supplies a genuine set-theoretic
function `ω → ω` (a set of pairs) satisfying the first pair of equations, and
`m +ω n` is its value at `n`; likewise for `·`.

The **arithmetic bridge** then shows that these set-theoretically defined
operations agree with Lean's built-in arithmetic under the correspondence
`vn : Nat → ω`: `vn (m + n) = vn m +ω vn n` and `vn (m * n) = vn m *ω vn n`.
This closes the loop begun in `Omega`: the natural numbers *with their
arithmetic* are faithfully represented by sets, and laws such as commutativity
can be transported along the bridge.


## Addition 

## Multiplication

# Cardinality: countable and uncountable

Cantor's great discovery was that infinite collections come in different sizes.
Two collections have the *same size* (are **equinumerous**) when there is a
one-to-one correspondence between them; a collection is **countable** when it
can be injected into the natural numbers — when its members can be tagged by
distinct numbers.

In this file we work with Lean types rather than ZF sets, since that is where
these facts are used later in the project. We show:

* **ℕ × ℕ ≃ ℕ**, by Cantor's explicit pairing function, which walks through the
  grid of pairs diagonal by diagonal: `(0,0), (1,0), (0,1), (2,0), (1,1), …`.
  So "infinitely many infinities of numbers" are no more than the numbers.
* The integers and finite lists of naturals are countable.
* A countable union of countable collections is countable (this needs the axiom
  of choice, to pick an enumeration of each piece simultaneously).
* **α < 𝒫(α)**: every type injects into its power type `α → Prop`, but nothing
  injects back — Cantor's theorem in its sharpest form.
* **ℕ → Bool is uncountable**: the infinite binary sequences (equivalently, the
  real numbers in binary) cannot be listed. This is Cantor's diagonal argument.


## Equinumerosity 

## Cantor's pairing function

# Zorn's lemma and the well-ordering theorem

The axiom of choice says that from any family of non-empty collections one may
choose one member of each, all at once. It is innocent-looking yet powerful,
and historically contested. Two of its most useful equivalents are:

* **Zorn's lemma**: in a partial order in which every chain (totally ordered
  part) has an upper bound, there is a maximal element.
* **Zermelo's well-ordering theorem** (1904): every collection can be
  well-ordered — arranged in a line in which every non-empty part has a first
  element.

Lean's logic includes choice (`Classical.choice`), so here we *derive* these
principles from it. The proof of Zorn avoids ordinals altogether. We work with
chains themselves: `succChain` enlarges a chain to a strictly bigger chain, when
one exists (a choice). The *tower* (`ChainClosure`) is the smallest family of
chains closed under `succChain` and under unions. A beautiful argument (going
back to Zermelo's second proof, and to Bourbaki, Witt and Kneser) shows that the
tower is itself linearly ordered by inclusion. Its union is then a chain that
`succChain` cannot enlarge — a *maximal* chain — and any upper bound of a
maximal chain is a maximal element.

Zermelo's theorem then follows from Zorn: consider well-orderings of parts of
the given type, ordered by "is an initial segment of". Chains have unions as
upper bounds; a maximal partial well-ordering must cover everything, since
otherwise a missing element could be appended at the end.

# Successor and limit ordinals; transfinite induction

Counting past the finite, one meets two kinds of ordinal. Some are reached by a
single step from a predecessor — the **successor** ordinals `α + 1 = α ∪ {α}`.
Others, like `ω`, have no immediate predecessor: they are reached only as the
"limit" of everything before them, and as von Neumann sets they are simply the
union of all smaller ordinals. Every ordinal is exactly one of: zero, a
successor, or a limit.

This trichotomy is what makes **transfinite induction** usable in practice: to
prove a property of all ordinals, show it for `0`, show that it passes from `α`
to `α + 1`, and show that it passes to a limit from everything below. We derive
both the general (course-of-values) form, from ∈-induction, and this three-case
form. We also show that the union of any set of ordinals is an ordinal — its
supremum — so that limits always exist.

# Comparing sizes: the comparability of cardinals

Cantor took it for granted that any two collections can be compared in size:
either the first fits into the second, or the second into the first. Without the
axiom of choice this cannot be proved — in fact Hartogs showed in 1915 that
comparability is *equivalent* to the axiom of choice. With choice (here in the
form of Zorn's lemma, proved in `Choice.lean`) it is a theorem:

* **Comparability.** For any two types `α` and `β`, there is an injection
  `α → β` or an injection `β → α`.

The proof considers *partial injections* from `α` to `β`: one-to-one
correspondences between a part of `α` and a part of `β`, recorded as a relation.
Ordered by inclusion they satisfy the hypothesis of Zorn's lemma (the union of a
chain of partial injections is again one), so there is a maximal one. If it left
out both a point `a` of `α` and a point `b` of `β`, we could add the pair
`(a, b)` and enlarge it; so it either uses up all of `α` — giving an injection
`α → β` — or all of `β` — giving an injection `β → α`.

Together with the Schröder–Bernstein theorem this makes "is at most as large as"
(`CardLE`) a **total preorder** on types whose associated equivalence is
equinumerosity: the sizes of collections form a linear order — the order of the
cardinal numbers.

# What it means to be infinite

There are two classical ways to say that a collection is infinite.

* **Not finite**: it cannot be counted off as `0, 1, …, n - 1` for any `n`; we say
  a type is *finite* when it injects into `Fin n = {0, …, n - 1}` for some `n`.
* **Dedekind-infinite**: it can be mapped one-to-one onto a *proper part* of
  itself. Galileo had noticed, puzzled, that the square numbers are in
  one-to-one correspondence with all numbers; Dedekind (1888) turned the paradox
  into a definition.

A third, more concrete property is that the natural numbers **embed** in the
collection (`ℕ ↪ α`). Here we prove that all three agree:

* `ℕ ↪ α` ⇒ Dedekind-infinite: shift the copy of `ℕ` one step along, `n ↦ n + 1`,
  and leave everything else fixed; the first point of the copy is missed.
* Dedekind-infinite ⇒ `ℕ ↪ α`: take a point `a` that `f` misses and follow its
  orbit `a, f a, f (f a), …`; the orbit never repeats.
* `ℕ ↪ α` ⇒ not finite: this is the **pigeonhole principle** — `n + 1` pigeons
  do not fit injectively into `n` holes — proved by induction on `n`.
* not finite ⇒ `ℕ ↪ α`: here the **axiom of choice** enters (in its weak,
  "dependent" form). Since no finite list exhausts `α`, we can keep choosing new
  points: having chosen `a₀, …, aₙ₋₁`, choose `aₙ` outside the list.

Without some choice, "infinite but Dedekind-finite" sets are consistent with ZF;
so the last step is not a mere technicality.

# The arithmetic of the infinite: κ · κ = κ

For finite numbers, multiplication makes things bigger: `n · n > n` once `n > 1`.
For infinite sizes Cantor found the opposite. Already `ℕ × ℕ ≃ ℕ`
(`Cardinality.lean`): a grid of numbers, infinite in two directions, can be
listed in a single sequence. The great generalisation, due to Hessenberg (1906)
for well-ordered sets and hence, with the axiom of choice, to all sets, is

* **κ · κ = κ for every infinite κ**: for any infinite type `α`, `α × α ≃ α`.

From it the whole of infinite cardinal arithmetic collapses into a single rule:
the sum and the product of two sizes, at least one of them infinite, is simply
the larger of the two (`α ⊕ β ≃ α × β ≃ max(α, β)`).

**The proof.** We follow Zorn's lemma once more. Fix a copy `e : ℕ ↪ α` of the
natural numbers inside `α`. Consider *partial squarings*: a part `A` of `α`
containing the copy of `ℕ`, together with an injection `A × A → A` (recorded as a
relation). The copy of `ℕ` itself carries one, by Cantor's pairing function, and
the union of a chain of partial squarings is again one; so Zorn gives a maximal
partial squaring with part `A`. Now compare `A` with its complement `C`
(comparability, `CardinalOrder.lean`):

* If `A` fits into `C`, say via `g`, let `B = g(A)`, a copy of `A` outside `A`.
  The new pairs in `(A ∪ B) × (A ∪ B)` — those not already in `A × A` — are at
  most as many as `(A ⊕ A) × (A ⊕ A)`, hence (using the injection `A × A → A`
  twice over) at most as many as `A`, hence as `B`. So we can send the new pairs
  injectively into `B` and enlarge the partial squaring — contradicting
  maximality.
* So `C` fits into `A`; then all of `α = A ∪ C` fits into `A ⊕ A`, hence into
  `A`, and `α × α` fits into `A × A`, hence into `A ⊆ α`. Schröder–Bernstein
  turns the injection `α × α → α` into a bijection.

# Hartogs' theorem: an ordinal beyond every set

Cantor's theorem produces, for every collection, a bigger one — its power set.
But the power set need not be *well-ordered*, and without the axiom of choice we
cannot compare it with other sizes. Hartogs (1915) found a different way up,
which needs no choice at all:

* **Hartogs' theorem.** For every collection `α` there is an ordinal `ℵ(α)` that
  does **not** inject into `α`; indeed `ℵ(α)` is exactly the set of ordinals that
  do inject into `α`, so it is the *least* ordinal that does not.

The idea is to collect all the ways of well-ordering parts of `α`. Each such
well-ordering `R` has an *order type*, an ordinal computed by the "collapse"
`rank R a = {rank R b | b R a}`, which replaces each point by the set of the
(collapsed) points before it, and the order type of `R` is the set of all ranks.
By the replacement axiom the order types of all well-orderings of parts of `α`
form a set, `ℵ(α)`. It is downward closed (an initial segment of a well-ordering
is a well-ordering), so it is an ordinal. Every ordinal `o` that injects into `α`
lies in `ℵ(α)`, since the injection copies the order of `o` onto a part of `α`,
and the collapse of that copy gives back `o` itself. So if `ℵ(α)` injected into
`α`, we would have `ℵ(α) ∈ ℵ(α)` — impossible by foundation.

Instead of well-orderings we use the slightly more general *transitive
well-founded relations*; this costs nothing and spares us from proving totality.

**On choice.** Mathematically the argument makes no choices: it uses only
replacement, power set (in the form "all relations on `α`"), foundation and
classical logic. In this project, however, ZF sets are modelled as a quotient of
pre-sets, and the set-forming operation `ofFamily` (our replacement) picks
representatives with `Classical.choice`; moreover Lean derives excluded middle
from `Classical.choice`. So `#print axioms` on these theorems does list
`Classical.choice` — the goal of a choice-free proof is achieved *at the level of
the mathematics*, but not as a formal axiom check. (The one place below where
we genuinely choose — turning a member of `ℵ(α)` back into an injection — is in
`mem_hartogs_iff`, and is only needed for the "least" part.)

The theorem is stated for `α : Type`, the universe from which our ZF sets draw
their members.

# Beyond: the tower of powers and Kőnig's theorem

Cantor's theorem `α < 𝒫(α)` (`Cardinality.lean`) can be applied again and again:
starting from the natural numbers we get an endless tower of ever larger
infinities

  `ℕ < 𝒫(ℕ) < 𝒫(𝒫(ℕ)) < 𝒫(𝒫(𝒫(ℕ))) < ⋯`

(`𝒫(ℕ)` has the size of the continuum, the real line). So the infinite is not
one thing but an unbounded hierarchy.

**Kőnig's theorem** (Julius Kőnig, 1905) is the most general form of Cantor's
diagonal argument. If for every index `i` the size `κᵢ` is strictly smaller than
`μᵢ`, then the sum `Σᵢ κᵢ` is strictly smaller than the product `Πᵢ μᵢ`. The
proof is a diagonal argument in many coordinates at once: given any map from the
sum to the product, at coordinate `i` the `κᵢ`-many functions coming from the
`i`-th summand cannot exhaust `μᵢ`, so we may choose a value they all miss; the
function made of these choices is hit by nothing. Cantor's theorem is the case
where all `κᵢ = 1` and all `μᵢ = 2`. (Kőnig used the theorem — erroneously — at
the 1904 Heidelberg congress to "refute" the continuum hypothesis' cousin, that
the continuum can be well-ordered; Zermelo's well-ordering theorem followed weeks
later.)

# The natural numbers, from Peano's axioms

This file begins Part II of the project: the *number systems*. Everything starts with the
natural numbers `0, 1, 2, …`, and we build them in the most austere way possible, following
Dedekind and Peano. A natural number is either

* `zero`, or
* `succ n`, the *successor* ("the next one after") of a natural number `n`.

Nothing else is a natural number, and every natural number arises in exactly one way from these
two clauses. In Lean this is literally an *inductive type*: the type is *generated* by its
constructors. Philosophically this is a striking stance: the numbers are not abstracted from
collections of things, but are the free result of a starting point and a "next" operation.
The principle of mathematical induction is then not an extra axiom but simply the statement that
there is nothing in the type beyond what the two clauses produce.

From this bare skeleton we define addition, multiplication, and the order `≤` by *recursion*
and prove all the familiar laws (associativity, commutativity, distributivity, cancellation, …)
by *induction*. We also prove the **well-ordering principle**: every nonempty collection of
natural numbers has a least element.

Finally we prove a **bridge theorem**: our home-made numbers `N` are isomorphic to Lean's
built-in natural numbers `Nat`, by an explicit bijection preserving `0`, successor, `+`, `×` and
`≤`. This licenses us, in all later files, to use Lean's `Nat` (and its efficient decision
procedure `omega`) freely: it is *the same structure* as the one we built by hand.

# The integers as classes of pairs of naturals

In the natural numbers we can add but not always subtract: `3 - 5` has no answer. The integers
repair this, and the construction shows how mathematicians *create* new objects out of old ones
by an act of abstraction.

Think of a pair of natural numbers `(a, b)` as a *formal difference* "`a` minus `b`". Many pairs
describe the same difference: `(5, 3)`, `(7, 5)`, `(2, 0)` all mean "two". We declare two pairs
equivalent when they describe the same difference,

  `(a, b) ~ (c, d)  ↔  a + d = c + b`

(note that this definition only uses *addition* of naturals, so it makes sense before negative
numbers exist). An integer is then, by definition, an *equivalence class* of pairs: the integer
`-2` **is** the collection of all pairs `(0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 4), …`. This is Frege's and
Russell's method of *definition by abstraction*: rather than postulating a mysterious new entity
"minus two", we identify it with the class of all its representatives. In Lean this is a
`Quotient` type.

We define `0`, `1`, `+`, `−`, `×` and `≤` on representatives, check that the choice of
representative does not matter, and then prove the laws of a **commutative ring** and that `≤` is
a **linear order** compatible with addition and with multiplication by positive numbers.
Finally a **bridge theorem** identifies our integers with Lean's built-in `Int`, so that later
files may use `Int` (and the arithmetic decision procedures `omega` and `grind`) freely.

From here on we use Lean's `Nat` in place of the home-made `N` of the previous file, as licensed by
the bridge theorem `N.bridge_nat`.

# Elementary number theory: Euclid's legacy

Before moving on from the whole numbers to fractions, we pause to prove the classical results of
*arithmetic* in Euclid's *Elements* (Books VII and IX), now on a fully formal footing. Thanks to
the bridge theorems `N.bridge_nat` and `Z.bridge_int` we work with Lean's `Nat` and `Int`.

* **Euclid's algorithm** computes the greatest common divisor by repeated division with
  remainder: `gcd a 0 = a` and `gcd a b = gcd b (a mod b)`. We prove that it really is the
  greatest common divisor.
* **Bézout's identity**: the gcd of `a` and `b` is an integer combination `a·x + b·y`. This is
  where negative numbers earn their keep.
* **Euclid's lemma**: a prime dividing a product divides one of the factors. This is what makes
  primes the "atoms" of multiplication.
* **Infinitude of primes** (Euclid IX.20): for every `n` there is a prime `p ≥ n`, found among the
  prime factors of `n! + 1`.
* **The fundamental theorem of arithmetic**: every positive integer is a product of primes, in
  exactly one way up to the order of the factors. Factorisations are represented as lists of
  primes, and "up to order" means "up to permutation of the list".

# The rational numbers as classes of fractions

The integers let us subtract; the rationals let us *divide*. The construction repeats the trick
used for the integers, one level up. A *fraction* is a pair `(n, d)` of integers with `d > 0`,
read as "`n` divided by `d`". Different fractions can name the same quantity — `1/2`, `2/4`,
`(-3)/(-6)` — and we declare

  `n/d ~ n'/d'  ↔  n · d' = n' · d`  ("cross-multiplication"),

which again only uses operations (here: multiplication of integers) that already exist. A
rational number **is** the class of all fractions equivalent to a given one: the number one-half
*is* the collection `{1/2, 2/4, 3/6, …}`. Every operation is defined on representatives and shown
not to depend on the choice of representative.

We prove that `Q` is an **ordered field**: the field axioms (including inverses of non-zero
elements) and an order compatible with `+` and with multiplication by positives. Having done so,
we *register* these facts with Lean's automation (`Lean.Grind.Field`, `Lean.Grind.OrderedRing`,
…), so that from then on the `grind` tactic can do routine algebra and linear inequalities in `Q`
for us. We then prove:

* the **Archimedean property**: every rational is below some natural number;
* **density**: between two rationals there is always a third;
* the **irrationality of √2**: no rational `q` satisfies `q · q = 2`.

The last fact is the ancient discovery, attributed to the Pythagoreans, that the rationals have
*gaps*. Filling those gaps is the task of the real numbers, constructed in the following files.

# Cauchy sequences of rationals

The rationals have gaps: no rational squares to `2`. Yet we can *approach* the missing point as
closely as we like — `1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, …` — by rationals whose squares tend to `2`. The idea
of Cauchy (and of Cantor and Méray, who turned it into a construction of the reals) is to take
such approximating processes themselves as the new numbers.

A sequence `a₀, a₁, a₂, …` of rationals is **Cauchy** if its terms eventually stay arbitrarily
close to *each other*:

  for every rational `ε > 0` there is an `N` such that `|aₘ − aₙ| < ε` whenever `m, n ≥ N`.

Crucially this definition does not mention any limit: it describes a sequence that "ought to
converge" using only the rationals themselves. Two Cauchy sequences are **equivalent** when their
difference tends to `0`, i.e. when they are "aiming at the same point". In the next file a real
number is *defined* to be an equivalence class of Cauchy sequences — once more the method of
definition by abstraction, this time applied to infinite processes rather than pairs.

In this file we develop what is needed about rationals and Cauchy sequences: the absolute value,
the equivalence relation, boundedness, and the arithmetic operations (sum, negation, product) on
Cauchy sequences, together with their compatibility with equivalence.

# The real numbers as classes of Cauchy sequences

We now take the decisive step of the Cantor–Méray construction. A **real number** is an
equivalence class of Cauchy sequences of rationals, two sequences being identified when their
difference tends to zero. The number `√2`, for instance, *is* the class of all rational sequences
that close in on it — `1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, …` and every other sequence equivalent to that one.

This may look like a sleight of hand: we wanted a *point* filling the gap and we were handed a
*process* instead. But this is the same move as before. The integer `−2` was the class of pairs
with difference `−2`, the rational `½` was the class of fractions equal to `½`; the real `√2` is
the class of rational processes converging to `√2`. In each case the new object is constituted
by everything that "points at it", and no prior existence of the object is presupposed.

In this file we define the real numbers `R`, the embedding `ofQ : Q → R` of the rationals as
constant sequences, and addition, negation and multiplication (computed term by term). The ring
laws are inherited directly from those of `Q`, because they hold term by term. We register `R`
with Lean's automation as a commutative ring. The order, the inverse, and the field structure
follow in `RealOrder.lean`.

# The order on the reals, inverses, and the ordered field ℝ

When is a real number *positive*? A Cauchy sequence may wobble, so we cannot just ask that its
terms be positive. The right notion is that the sequence is **eventually bounded away from zero
from above**: from some point on, all its terms exceed some fixed positive rational `ε`. This
does not depend on the representative, so it defines positivity of real numbers, and we set
`x < y` iff `y − x` is positive.

The key fact is **trichotomy**: every real is positive, zero, or negative. Its proof uses
classical logic in an essential way — given a Cauchy sequence, we cannot in general *decide* in
finitely many steps whether it converges to `0` (a famous point of Brouwer's intuitionist
critique). Classically, though, if a sequence does *not* tend to zero then it is eventually
bounded away from zero, and so is eventually positive or eventually negative.

Next, inverses. If `x ≠ 0` its representing sequence is eventually bounded away from zero, so
inverting it term by term gives again a Cauchy sequence, which represents `1/x`. We then define
`x⁻¹` as "the" `y` with `x · y = 1` (chosen by the axiom of choice, the junk value `0⁻¹ = 0`
otherwise) — this avoids any need to check well-definedness by hand.

The upshot is that **ℝ is an ordered field**, registered with Lean's automation. We also prove
the **Archimedean property** of ℝ and a few lemmas relating reals and the rationals inside them
(the embedding `ofQ` preserves order; every positive real exceeds a positive rational; a Cauchy
sequence is approximated by its own terms), which prepare the proof of completeness.

# Bisection: manufacturing Cauchy sequences

To prove that the reals have no gaps we must *produce* real numbers, that is, Cauchy sequences of
rationals. The simplest machine for doing so is the ancient method of **bisection** (interval
halving), familiar from the search for a word in a dictionary.

Suppose `P` is some property of rationals, `l ≤ u`, `P` fails at `l` and holds at `u`. Look at
the midpoint `m = (l + u)/2`. If `P m` holds, keep the left half `[l, m]`; otherwise keep the
right half `[m, u]`. Either way we again have an interval whose left end fails `P` and whose right
end satisfies it, now of half the length. Repeating forever gives nested intervals
`[lₙ, uₙ]` of length `(u − l)/2ⁿ`.

Because the intervals shrink to nothing (by the Archimedean property, `2ⁿ` eventually exceeds any
bound), both endpoint sequences are Cauchy, and they are equivalent: they define *one* real
number, the "cut point" where `P` switches from false to true. Note that the choice at each step
("does `P m` hold?") need not be computable; we use classical logic to make it.

This file sets up the machine in general; `Completeness.lean` feeds it the properties
"`q` is an upper bound of `S`" (to obtain least upper bounds) and "`q² ≥ 2`" (to obtain `√2`).

# Completeness of the reals, and the existence of √2

This file proves the property that distinguishes the reals from the rationals and was the whole
point of the construction: **completeness**. In Dedekind's formulation, the line has no gaps;
in the form we prove, *every nonempty set of reals that is bounded above has a least upper bound*
(a *supremum*).

A set of reals is represented as a predicate `S : R → Prop` ("`x` belongs to the set iff
`S x`"). The proof feeds the bisection machine of `Bisection.lean` with the property
"`q` is an upper bound of `S`": starting from a rational below some element of `S` and a rational
upper bound, bisection traps the supremum in ever smaller intervals, and the Cauchy sequence of
right endpoints *is* (represents) the least upper bound.

As a first payoff we show that `√2` exists in `R`: there is a real `r > 0` with `r · r = 2`.
Here too we use bisection, this time on the property "`q² ≥ 2`", and check directly that the
resulting real squares to `2`. Thus the gap in the rationals discovered by the Pythagoreans is
filled.

# The reals are uncountable; the rationals are not complete

Two contrasts close the construction of the number line.

**Cantor's theorem on the continuum (1874).** The natural numbers, the integers and the
rationals can all be listed in a single infinite sequence. The reals cannot: given *any*
sequence `f 0, f 1, f 2, …` of reals, some real is missing from it. We follow Cantor's original
*nested intervals* argument. Start with `[0, 1]`. At step `n`, cut the current interval into
thirds; the number `f n` cannot lie in both the lower and the upper third, so keep a third
that avoids it. The intervals are nested, so by completeness (the least upper bound of the left
endpoints) there is a real `L` in all of them — and `L` differs from every `f n`. So there are
"more" reals than natural numbers: the infinite comes in different sizes.

**The rationals are not complete.** Conversely, the property proved in `Completeness.lean`
genuinely fails one level down: the set `{q ∈ ℚ | q² < 2}` is nonempty and bounded above, yet has
no least upper bound *in ℚ*. Its supremum "should" be `√2`, which is irrational. This is precisely
the gap that the passage from `Q` to `R` fills.

# ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ

Strictly speaking, our constructions do not make the natural numbers a *subset* of the integers:
an integer is a class of pairs of naturals, not a natural number. What is true is that each
system contains a faithful *copy* of the previous one: there is an injective map preserving
`0`, `1`, `+` and `×` (and the order). This is how the familiar chain `ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ` is to be
understood in a construction-based foundation: "`3` is a real number" means that the real number
represented by the constant sequence `3, 3, 3, …` plays, among the reals, exactly the role that
the natural number `3` plays among the naturals.

* `ℕ → ℤ` sends `n` to the class of the pair `(n, 0)`;
* `ℤ → ℚ` sends an integer `i` to the class of the fraction `i/1`;
* `ℚ → ℝ` sends `q` to the class of the constant sequence `q, q, q, …`.
