# Degree, division with remainder, and roots

Schoolchildren learn to divide polynomials by long division; Euclid (Elements VII) divided
numbers. Both are instances of a single structural fact, the **division algorithm**: given
`g` with invertible leading coefficient, every `p` can be written `p = q·g + r` with `r` of
smaller degree than `g`. It is the engine behind the next file, where rings with such an
algorithm (Euclidean domains) are shown to have principal ideals.

Two classical corollaries close this file.

* **The factor theorem** (Descartes, *La Géométrie*, 1637): `a` is a root of `p` exactly when
  `x - a` divides `p`. Division by `x - a` leaves the constant remainder `p(a)`.
* **A polynomial of degree `n` has at most `n` roots** in an integral domain — a fact
  Lagrange used in 1768 to prove that `x^(p-1) - 1` factors completely mod `p`. Each root
  splits off a linear factor and lowers the degree by one; the absence of zero divisors
  ensures that no new roots appear along the way.

Instead of a degree *function* with a special value for the zero polynomial, the basic notion
here is the predicate `DegLT p d` — "all coefficients from index `d` on vanish" — from which
the length `len p` (one more than the degree, and `0` for the zero polynomial), the degree
`natDegree p` and the leading coefficient are derived.

# Euclidean domains and principal ideal domains

Euclid's algorithm for the greatest common divisor rests on one property of the integers:
one can always divide with a remainder *smaller* than the divisor. The same is true for
polynomials over a field (previous file). Rings with such a division, measured by some
"size" in the natural numbers, are called **Euclidean domains**.

Dedekind's ideals were invented to restore unique factorisation where it fails; in a
Euclidean domain it never fails, because every ideal is generated by a single element — the
ring is a **principal ideal domain (PID)**. The proof is the abstract form of Euclid's
algorithm: an ideal is generated by any of its non-zero elements of least size, for the
remainder of anything else on division by it would be smaller still.

In a PID the two possible meanings of "prime number" coincide. An **irreducible** element
admits no non-trivial factorisation (the schoolbook definition); a **prime** element `p` has
the property `p ∣ ab ⇒ p ∣ a or p ∣ b` (Euclid's lemma, Elements VII.30). Prime always implies
irreducible in a domain; that irreducible implies prime is precisely what fails in
Kummer's rings of cyclotomic integers, and it is the key to unique factorisation. We prove
it for every PID — in particular for `ℤ` and for `F[x]`.

# Unique factorisation

The **fundamental theorem of arithmetic** — every integer `n ≥ 2` is a product of primes,
uniquely up to order — is implicit in Euclid and was first stated and proved with full
clarity by Gauss in the *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* (1801). Its failure in rings such as
`ℤ[√-5]`, where `6 = 2 · 3 = (1 + √-5)(1 - √-5)`, was the crisis that led Kummer to "ideal
numbers" and Dedekind to ideals.

A factorisation theorem has two halves, and they rest on different foundations.

* **Uniqueness** follows from Euclid's lemma alone: in any integral domain in which every
  irreducible element is prime (in particular in every PID, by the previous file), two
  factorisations of the same element into irreducibles agree up to order and unit factors.
  The proof is Euclid's: a prime factor on one side divides the product on the other, hence
  divides — and is associated to — one of its factors, which can then be cancelled.
* **Existence** is a finiteness property: factoring cannot go on forever. We prove it for
  `ℤ` (by induction on absolute value) and for `F[x]` over a field (by induction on degree).

Since factorisations are unique only "up to order and units", we compare them by counting,
for each `x`, how many factors are **associated** to `x` (equal to it up to a unit factor):
a factorisation is in effect a multiset of associate classes.

# The Gaussian integers

In his second memoir on biquadratic residues (1832) Gauss enlarged the integers to the
numbers `a + bi` with `a, b ∈ ℤ` and `i² = -1`, and showed that arithmetic there is as
well-behaved as in `ℤ`: there is division with small remainder, hence a Euclidean algorithm,
hence unique factorisation. It was the first time a "number system" had been invented to
illuminate questions about the ordinary integers — here, which primes are sums of two
squares, since `a² + b² = (a + bi)(a - bi)` — and it opened the road to algebraic number
theory.

The key quantity is the **norm** `N(a + bi) = a² + b²`, which is multiplicative. To divide
`α` by `β ≠ 0`, compute the exact quotient `α β̄ / N(β)` and round each coordinate to the
nearest integer; the rounding errors are at most `1/2`, so the remainder `ρ` satisfies
`N(ρ) ≤ N(β)/2 < N(β)`. Thus **`ℤ[i]` is a Euclidean domain**, and by the previous files a
PID with unique factorisation.

# Fermat's two-squares theorem

On Christmas Day 1640 Fermat wrote to Mersenne that every prime of the form `4k + 1` is a
sum of two squares — `5 = 1 + 4`, `13 = 4 + 9`, `17 = 1 + 16`, `29 = 4 + 25` — and, as usual,
offered no proof. Euler found one in 1749 after years of effort. The classical modern route
goes through the Gaussian integers `ℤ[i]`: they form a Euclidean domain, hence a PID, and
a prime `p ≡ 1 (mod 4)` cannot remain prime there.

We formalise instead the astonishing **"one-sentence proof"** of Don Zagier (1990), itself a
distillation of an argument of Heath-Brown, which uses nothing but counting:

> The involution on the finite set `S = {(x, y, z) ∈ ℕ³ : x² + 4yz = p}` defined by
> `(x, y, z) ↦ (x + 2z, z, y − x − z)` if `x < y − z`,
> `(2y − x, y, x − y + z)` if `y − z < x < 2y`, and
> `(x − 2y, x − y + z, y)` if `x > 2y`
> has exactly one fixed point, so `|S|` is odd, and the involution `(x, y, z) ↦ (x, z, y)`
> also has a fixed point.

A fixed point of the second involution has `y = z`, so `p = x² + (2y)²`. The parity
principle — *an involution on a finite set has as many fixed points as the set has
elements, modulo 2* — is the case `p = 2` of the fixed-point congruence for `p`-group actions
proved in `Action.lean`, applied to the group `ℤ/2ℤ`. It is a striking illustration of the
structural method: a theorem of number theory obtained from a theorem about group actions,
via a set constructed for the purpose.

# The untyped λ-calculus and the Church–Rosser theorem

In the 1930s Alonzo Church proposed the **λ-calculus** as a foundation for
logic and as an analysis of the notion of an *effectively calculable function*.
It has just three kinds of expression: variables, *application* `t u` ("apply
the function `t` to `u`"), and *abstraction* `λx. t` ("the function sending `x`
to `t`"). Computation is a single rule, **β-reduction**: `(λx. t) u ⟶ t[x := u]`,
substitute the argument for the parameter. Everything else — numbers,
booleans, pairs, recursion — can be *encoded* (Church numerals below).

Two things make the calculus delicate.

* **Variables and substitution.** Substituting must not capture free
  variables. Following N. G. de Bruijn (1972) we avoid names altogether: a
  variable is a number `n`, pointing to the `n`-th enclosing `λ`. So `λx. λy. x`
  is written `λ λ 1`. Substitution then becomes a purely mechanical operation
  on these numbers, with a small algebra of laws (`subst_subst` etc.).
* **Order of evaluation.** A term may contain several redexes; does the choice
  matter? The **Church–Rosser theorem** (1936) says no: if `t` reduces to `u`
  and to `v`, then `u` and `v` reduce to a common term. Hence normal forms, when
  they exist, are unique: a λ-term has at most one "value". We give the elegant
  proof of Tait and Martin-Löf, through *parallel reduction*, in the streamlined
  form of Takahashi: every term `t` has a *complete development* `cd t`
  (contract all its redexes at once), and any parallel step from `t` can be
  completed to `cd t` (the "triangle property").

Not every term has a normal form: `Ω = (λx. x x)(λx. x x)` reduces only to
itself. Computation can run forever — the price of the calculus' expressive
power (it is Turing-complete), and the reason why *typed* calculi, studied in
the following files, are needed when λ-terms are to serve as proofs.

# The simply typed λ-calculus

The untyped λ-calculus is too liberal to serve as a logic: Curry's paradox
(1942) and the Kleene–Rosser paradox (1935) showed that Church's original
system, which combined λ-terms with logical constants, was inconsistent, and
`Ω` shows that computation need not end. Church's remedy (1940) was to add
**types**, in the spirit of Russell's theory of types: every term gets a type,
and a function of type `A → B` may only be applied to an argument of type `A`.
Self-application `x x` becomes ill-typed, and with it `Ω`.

Here we study the **simply typed λ-calculus** with function types `A → B`,
products `A × B` (pairs, with projections), sums `A + B` (tagged alternatives,
with case analysis) and the empty type `⊥` (with "ex falso" elimination), over
a supply of atomic types. We present it *à la Curry*: terms are untyped (with
de Bruijn indices, as in `Lambda.lean`), and a separate judgement
`Γ ⊢ t : A` assigns types, where the context `Γ` lists the types of the free
variables `0, 1, 2, …`.

The two basic metatheorems, the slogan of which is Milner's *well-typed
programs cannot go wrong*, are:

* **Subject reduction (preservation).** Reduction preserves types: if
  `Γ ⊢ t : A` and `t ⟶ t'` then `Γ ⊢ t' : A`. The heart of the proof is the
  *substitution lemma*: substituting well-typed terms for variables preserves
  typing.
* **Progress.** A closed well-typed term is either a *value* (an introduction
  form: a `λ`, a pair, or an injection) or can take a step. A closed term never
  gets "stuck" in a meaningless state such as applying a pair to an argument.

Lean's own kernel is a vastly extended relative of this system — dependent
types, universes and inductive types — and its soundness rests on metatheorems
of exactly this kind.

# Strong normalization: Tait's method of reducibility

The simply typed λ-calculus has a property the untyped calculus lacks
spectacularly: **every reduction sequence of a well-typed term is finite**.
There is no `Ω`; every typed program terminates, whatever order of evaluation is
chosen (*strong* normalization). This was proved by W. W. Tait (1967), whose
method — later extended by Girard (1972) to System F with his "candidats de
réductibilité", and by Martin-Löf to his type theory — has become the
standard tool for such results.

**Why a naive proof fails.** One would like to prove "every typed term is
strongly normalizing" by induction on the term. The case of an application
`t u` breaks down: `t` and `u` may each terminate, yet `t u` can create a new
redex whose contraction substitutes `u` deep inside `t`, producing a larger
term. The induction hypothesis is too weak.

**Tait's idea.** Strengthen the claim, by recursion on the type, to a property
`RED A` ("reducible at type `A`") that is *closed under the elimination rule* of
`A` by definition:

* at an atom or `⊥`: `t` is strongly normalizing;
* at `A → B`: for every reducible `u` of type `A`, the application `t u` is
  reducible at `B`;
* at `A × B`: both projections are reducible;
* at `A + B`: `t` is strongly normalizing, and whatever injection it reduces to
  carries a reducible term.

One then checks Girard's three conditions — reducible terms are strongly
normalizing (CR1), reducibility is preserved by reduction (CR2), and a
*neutral* term (one that is not an introduction form) all of whose one-step
reducts are reducible is reducible (CR3) — and proves the **fundamental lemma**:
every well-typed term, with reducible terms substituted for its free variables,
is reducible. Substituting the variables themselves (which are reducible by
CR3) gives strong normalization.

Philosophically, `RED A` is a *semantics* of the type `A`: a meaning-explanation
in the style of the Brouwer–Heyting–Kolmogorov interpretation, where a proof of
`A → B` is a method transforming proofs of `A` into proofs of `B`. Normalization
is then soundness of the calculus for that semantics. Note that the definition
of `RED (A → B)` quantifies over `RED A`: the strength of the proof lies in this
quantification, which is why (by Gödel's second incompleteness theorem) such a
proof cannot be carried out in a much weaker system than the one in which `RED`
is defined.

**Consistency.** A closed term of type `⊥` would normalize to a closed normal
term of type `⊥`; but closed normal terms are values (`progress`), and no value
has type `⊥`. Read as logic (`CurryHoward.lean`), this says the calculus cannot
prove a contradiction.
**Constructive metatheory.** None of these proofs uses `Classical.choice` (and
hence none uses excluded middle): strong normalization is an accessibility
proof, and the passage to a normal form decides at each stage, with the
function `step?` of `STLC.lean`, whether another step is possible. So the
consistency of intuitionistic logic, and the unprovability of excluded middle
in `CurryHoward.lean`, are established by intuitionistically acceptable means —
as Brouwer and Heyting would have wished.

# Propositions as types: the Curry–Howard correspondence

Read the simple types as *formulas* of propositional logic: an atom is a
propositional variable, `A → B` is implication, `A × B` conjunction, `A + B`
disjunction, `⊥` falsity (and `¬A` abbreviates `A → ⊥`). Then the typing rules
of the simply typed λ-calculus are, letter for letter, the rules of Gentzen's
**natural deduction** (1934) for intuitionistic propositional logic, once the
terms are erased: `λ` is implication introduction, application is *modus
ponens*, pairing and projections are the rules for `∧`, injections and case
analysis the rules for `∨`, and `absurd` is *ex falso quodlibet*.

So a term of type `A` *is* a proof of `A`. This is the **Curry–Howard
correspondence**, observed by Curry (1934, for combinators and Hilbert-style
axioms) and made precise by Howard (1969, circulated as a manuscript, published
1980) for natural deduction. It gives formal content to the
**Brouwer–Heyting–Kolmogorov** explanation of the intuitionistic connectives: a
proof of `A → B` is a construction transforming proofs of `A` into proofs of
`B`; a proof of `A ∨ B` is a proof of one of them *together with the
information which one*; there is no proof of `⊥`.

The correspondence goes deeper than provability. **Computation is proof
simplification**: a β-redex `(λx. t) u` is an introduction immediately followed
by an elimination — a detour, or *cut*, in the proof — and contracting it is
Prawitz's (1965) step of normalization of natural deduction proofs. A normal
term is a *normal* (cut-free) proof, which has the *subformula property*. So
the normalization theorem of `Normalization.lean` *is* the cut-elimination (or
normalization) theorem for intuitionistic natural deduction.

We prove:

* **Curry–Howard**: `Γ ⊢ A` in natural deduction iff some term has type `A` in
  context `Γ` (erasing terms in one direction, extracting them in the other).
* **Normal terms ↔ normal proofs**: normal well-typed terms correspond to
  derivations in the *intercalation calculus* (`Nf`/`Ne`): introductions applied
  on top of chains of eliminations from hypotheses.
* **Cut elimination**: every provable formula has a normal proof — via
  normalization of terms.
* Consequences read off from the shape of normal proofs: intuitionistic logic
  is consistent and does not prove the **law of excluded middle** `A ∨ ¬A`,
  **Peirce's law** `((A → B) → A) → A` (for distinct atoms `A`, `B`), or
  **double-negation elimination** `¬¬A → A` (here the normal-form analysis is
  combined with soundness for classical truth tables) — although it does prove
  `¬¬(A ∨ ¬A)`, for which we exhibit the term.
  Brouwer's rejection of excluded middle thus becomes a theorem about a formal
  system.

Lean itself rests on the same idea, scaled up: in its dependent type theory

# System F: polymorphism, and why `Type : Type` fails

In the simply typed λ-calculus the identity function must be written once for
every type: `λx. x : A → A`, `λx. x : B → B`, … **System F**, discovered
independently by Jean-Yves Girard (1972, as a proof-theoretic tool for
second-order arithmetic) and John Reynolds (1974, as a theory of polymorphic
programs), lets terms abstract over *types*: the polymorphic identity
`Λα. λx. x` has type `∀α. α → α`, and can be instantiated at any type, including
`∀α. α → α` itself. This *impredicativity* — a quantifier over all types that
itself denotes a type — makes the system immensely expressive: natural numbers
(`∀α. (α → α) → α → α`), pairs, sums, lists and every function provably total in
second-order arithmetic are definable.

Under Curry–Howard, System F is second-order intuitionistic propositional logic,
and Girard proved its normalization by extending Tait's method with
*reducibility candidates*: since `∀α. A` quantifies over all types, its
reducibility must quantify over all *possible* reducibility predicates. (We do
not formalize that proof here; it needs the impredicative quantification that
Lean's `Prop` happens to offer.)

Here we set up System F à la Church-for-types (explicit type abstraction `Λ.`
and type application `t [B]`, with de Bruijn indices for both term and type
variables) and prove **subject reduction** and **progress**. Two layers of
substitution interact: substituting a type for a type variable inside a typing
derivation (`HasType.tySubst`) requires that type substitution commute with
the shifting of contexts under a `Λ`.

**Why not `Type : Type`?** One might go further and let types be terms of a type
of all types, `Type : Type` (Martin-Löf's first, 1971, version of his type
theory did exactly this). Girard showed in 1972 that this is inconsistent —
every type, including the empty type, becomes inhabited — by encoding the
Burali-Forti paradox of the ordinal of all ordinals; Hurkens (1995) simplified
the paradox to a short term. The proof is a type-theoretic shadow of Russell's
and Burali-Forti's paradoxes (cf. `Paradoxes.lean`, `Ordinals.lean` in Part I),
and it is the reason why Lean, like Martin-Löf's later theories and Coq, has an
infinite hierarchy of *universes* `Type 0 : Type 1 : Type 2 : ⋯` instead of a
single type of all types, with impredicativity confined to `Prop`. (We state the
paradox here only informally; a formal derivation is beyond this part.)

# System F: the algebra of two substitutions

System F has two kinds of variables — for terms and for types — and therefore
two substitution operations, which interact: substituting a term under a type
abstraction `Λ` must shift the type variables of the substituted term, and
substituting a type into a term must commute with substituting terms. This file
proves the necessary laws (the "σ-calculus" of de Bruijn substitutions, twice
over), shows that reduction is stable under both substitutions, and gives a
*decision procedure* `step?` for whether a term can reduce. These are the tools
for Girard's normalization proof in `SystemFNormalization.lean`.

None of this has philosophical content of its own; it is the bookkeeping that
pen-and-paper proofs dismiss with "by the usual properties of substitution" —
and which a proof assistant insists on seeing.

# Girard's theorem: strong normalization of System F

Tait's method (`Normalization.lean`) defines, for each type, the set of
*reducible* terms by recursion on the type. For System F this breaks down at the
quantifier: a term of type `∀α. A` can be instantiated at *any* type `B`,
including types far larger than `∀α. A` itself (for instance `∀α. A` again), so
"reducible at `∀α. A`" cannot be defined from "reducible at `A[B]`" by recursion
on types. This is impredicativity, and it is exactly what makes the system
strong.

**Girard's solution** (1972): do not try to say *which* set of terms `α`
denotes. Instead quantify over *all* sets of terms that could serve: the
**reducibility candidates** — predicates on terms satisfying Tait's three
conditions (CR1) members are strongly normalizing, (CR2) closure under
reduction, (CR3) a neutral term all of whose reducts are members is a member.
A type with free type variables is interpreted relative to an *environment*
`ρ` assigning a candidate to each type variable:

* `⟦α⟧ρ = ρ(α)`;
* `⟦A → B⟧ρ = { t | ∀ u ∈ ⟦A⟧ρ, t u ∈ ⟦B⟧ρ }`;
* `⟦∀α. A⟧ρ = { t | for every type B and every candidate C, t [B] ∈ ⟦A⟧(ρ, α ↦ C) }`.

The last clause quantifies over *all candidates* — a quantification over sets of
terms that includes the very set being defined. In Lean this is possible
because `Prop` is impredicative: `∀ C : Cand, …` is again a proposition. (By
Gödel's second incompleteness theorem the proof cannot be formalized in
second-order arithmetic, whose consistency it implies: Girard's theorem shows
that the functions provably total there are exactly those definable in
System F.)

The key lemmas are that each `⟦A⟧ρ` is a candidate, and the **substitution
lemma** `⟦A[B]⟧ρ = ⟦A⟧(ρ, α ↦ ⟦B⟧ρ)`, which is where the impredicative
quantification pays off in the case of type application. The **fundamental
lemma** then states that a well-typed term, with reducible terms substituted for
its free variables (and any types for its type variables), lies in the
interpretation of its type.

**Corollary: consistency.** The type `∀α. α` — under Curry–Howard the
second-order proposition "everything is true", i.e. falsity — has no closed
inhabitant. Its normal form would have to be `Λ. s` with `s` a closed normal term
of the bare type variable `α`, and there is none. The proofs in this file use
no choice; excluded middle is not needed either, since normality is decidable
(`step?`).

# Impredicativity at work: Church encodings in System F

In System F the data types of programming need not be added: they can be
*defined*, by the same trick Church used in the untyped calculus, now with
types. The idea (due to Böhm–Berarducci and Girard) is that a data type *is* its
own iteration principle:

* `Bool := ∀α. α → α → α` — a boolean is a way of choosing between two
  alternatives of any type; `true := Λα. λx. λy. x`, `false := Λα. λx. λy. y`.
* `Nat := ∀α. (α → α) → α → α` — a natural number `n` is the operation of
  iterating any function `n` times: `n̄ := Λα. λf. λx. fⁿ x`.
* `A × B := ∀α. (A → B → α) → α` — a pair is something that can feed its two
  components to any two-argument consumer.

The quantifier `∀α` ranges over *all* types, including `Nat` itself. That is
what makes these definitions work — `n̄ [Nat]` iterates a function on numbers,
which is how addition and multiplication are defined — and also what makes them
philosophically striking: the type `Nat` is defined by quantifying over a
totality to which it belongs. Poincaré and Russell regarded such *impredicative*
definitions as viciously circular; Ramsey and Gödel defended them on the ground
that they merely single out an object that already exists. Girard's
normalization theorem (`SystemFNormalization.lean`) shows that, at least, they
cannot lead to non-terminating computation or to a proof of falsity.

We give the encodings with their typing derivations, and check that they
compute: the successor of `n̄` reduces to the numeral of `n + 1`, iteration
unfolds to `fⁿ x`, the conditional selects the right branch, and projections
recover the components of a pair.

# Part V: Types — examining the ground floor

The whole project is written in Lean, whose logic is a dependent type theory.
This part turns around and studies small type theories as mathematical objects:
the untyped λ-calculus of Church with the Church–Rosser theorem; the simply
typed λ-calculus with subject reduction and progress; Tait's strong
normalization proof by reducibility, and the consistency it implies; the
Curry–Howard correspondence between simply typed terms and intuitionistic
natural deduction proofs, with cut elimination and the unprovability of
excluded middle, Peirce's law and double-negation elimination; and Girard and
Reynolds' polymorphic System F, with an account of why `Type : Type` is
inconsistent, Girard's strong normalization theorem for System F by
reducibility candidates (hence its consistency), and the impredicative Church
encodings of booleans, numbers and pairs. All metatheory here is constructive:
normality is decidable, and no use is made of `Classical.choice`.

# Tarski's axioms for plane geometry

Euclid's *Elements* (c. 300 BC) was for two thousand years the model of a
deductive science, yet its proofs rely on facts nowhere stated — that two
circles meet, that a line entering a triangle must leave it. Hilbert's
*Grundlagen der Geometrie* (1899) repaired this with twenty axioms in several
sorts (points, lines, planes) and primitive relations of incidence, order and
congruence. Alfred Tarski (lectures of 1926–27, published 1959; the definitive
system in Schwabhäuser–Szmielew–Tarski, *Metamathematische Methoden in der
Geometrie*, 1983) went further: **one sort** (points) and **two relations**,

* *betweenness* `B a b c` — "`b` lies on the segment from `a` to `c`" (endpoints
  allowed), and
* *equidistance* `a b ≡ c d` — "the segment `ab` is as long as `cd`".

Lines, circles, angles and triangles are all *defined*. The axioms below are
those of Tarski's system for the plane:

1. reflexivity of congruence `ab ≡ ba`; 2. its (pseudo-)transitivity;
3. identity: `ab ≡ cc` only if `a = b`; 4. **segment construction**: any
segment can be laid off on any ray; 5. the **five-segment axiom** (a form of
the side-angle-side congruence criterion); 6. identity of betweenness;
7. **Pasch's axiom** (inner form); 8.–9. lower and upper **dimension** axioms
(the space is exactly two-dimensional); 10. **Euclid's axiom** (in Tarski's
form, equivalent to the parallel postulate); 11. the **continuity** schema
(Dedekind cuts on lines have boundary points).

Tarski stated continuity as a schema of first-order formulas, so that his
*elementary geometry* is a first-order theory; he proved it **complete and
decidable** — every sentence about points, betweenness and equidistance is
either provable or refutable, and an algorithm decides which (by reduction to
the theory of real closed fields and quantifier elimination). We state
continuity more strongly, for arbitrary predicates (the second-order form, as
in Hilbert's completeness axiom); its models are, up to isomorphism, exactly
the planes over complete ordered fields, i.e. ℝ² (see `CartesianModel.lean`).

From the axioms we derive a few of the very first theorems of Tarski's
development: congruence is an equivalence relation, null segments are all
congruent, betweenness is symmetric, and so on — tiny facts, but here every
one must be *proved*, which is precisely the point.

# The Cartesian plane is a model of Tarski's axioms

Descartes' *La Géométrie* (1637) turned geometry into algebra: a point of the
plane is a pair of numbers `(x, y)`, and geometric relations become equations
between coordinates. Here we run Descartes' idea backwards to *justify* the
axioms: over any ordered field `K` we define

* `B a b c` iff `b = a + t (c − a)` for some `t` with `0 ≤ t ≤ 1`, and
* `ab ≡ cd` iff `|ab|² = |cd|²`, where `|ab|² = (a₁−b₁)² + (a₂−b₂)²`

(using *squared* distances, so that no square roots are needed), and check
Tarski's axioms one by one.

The outcome is instructive. **Nine of the eleven axioms hold in `K²` for every
ordered field `K`** — even for the rationals. The other two depend on the number
field:

* **segment construction** needs square roots of non-negative elements (to lay
  off a segment of length `√(|bc|²)` on a ray); it holds whenever `K` is
  *Euclidean* in this sense, for instance for `ℝ`;
* **continuity** needs the least-upper-bound property; it holds for `ℝ` by the
  completeness theorem of Part II.

Hence **`ℝ²` is a model of all of Tarski's axioms** — a relative consistency
proof: if the real numbers (built in Part II from the rationals, hence from the
natural numbers) are consistent, so is Euclidean geometry. This was Hilbert's
strategy in the *Grundlagen*. In `Euclid.lean` we see that `ℚ²` really does
fail both axioms: *which* geometry we get is fixed by the number field from
which the space is built.

# Euclid I.1, and why the rational plane is not enough

The very first proposition of Euclid's *Elements* reads: *on a given finite
straight line to construct an equilateral triangle.* Euclid draws the circle
with centre `A` through `B` and the circle with centre `B` through `A`, and
takes for `C` "the point in which the circles cut one another". He never
proves that there is such a point. Two thousand years later this gap, noticed
by Leibniz among others, became one of the motivations for Hilbert's axiom of
completeness and Dedekind's analysis of continuity.

In coordinates the gap is plain to see. For `A = (0, 0)` and `B = (1, 0)` the
two circles meet in `(1/2, ±√3/2)`. In the **real** plane these points exist,
because the reals have square roots (`euclid_I_1`). In the **rational** plane —
the plane of all points with rational coordinates, already infinitely dense,
and with all the same definitions — they do not, because `√3` is irrational
(`no_equilateral_rat`). The circles pass "through" each other without meeting.

So the rational plane satisfies most of Tarski's axioms (all the ones proved in
`CartesianModel.lean` for every ordered field), but fails:

* **segment construction**: the diagonal of the unit square, of length `√2`,
  cannot be laid off along the `x`-axis (`rat_not_segment_construction`);
* **continuity**: the points of the `x`-axis with `x² < 2` and those with
  `x² > 2` are separated by no rational point (`rat_not_continuous`).

The moral, which runs through modern geometry from Descartes to Hilbert, is
that a plane is fixed by its number field: the "same" axioms of incidence and
order yield different spaces over `ℚ`, over the constructible numbers, over the
real algebraic numbers, or over `ℝ`, and Euclid's constructions tacitly assume
enough of them.

# Pythagoras, Thales, and the triangle inequality

With coordinates, the classical metric theorems of plane geometry become
algebraic identities — Descartes' programme in miniature. The "angle at `b`"
between `a` and `c` is measured by the **dot product** `(a − b)·(c − b)`; it is
a right angle when the dot product vanishes.

* **The law of cosines** `|ac|² = |ab|² + |bc|² − 2 (a − b)·(c − b)` is a polynomial
  identity, and **Pythagoras' theorem** (Euclid I.47) and its converse (I.48)
  follow at once.
* **Thales' theorem**: a point `b` sees a segment `ac` at a right angle exactly when
  it lies on the circle with diameter `ac`.
* **Heron's formula**, in the squared form `16·Area² = 4|ab|²|ac|² − (|ab|² + |ac|² − |bc|²)²`,
  expresses the area through the sides.

These hold over every ordered field. The **triangle inequality**
`|ac| ≤ |ab| + |bc|` concerns lengths themselves, i.e. square roots, so we prove it
in `ℝ²`, via the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, which in turn comes from Lagrange's
identity `|u|²|v|² − (u·v)² = (u × v)²`.

Since the Babylonians (Plimpton 322, c. 1800 BC), Pythagoras' theorem has been
the bridge between geometry and arithmetic; it is also the reason why the
plane's distance is the square root of a sum of squares — the very formula with
which `CartesianModel.lean` *defined* congruence. Within the model, Pythagoras
is thus almost a tautology; its content lies in the fact that the model
satisfies Tarski's purely geometric axioms, from which (by Tarski's
completeness theorem) every such metric fact follows.

# Categories, functors and natural transformations

Category theory was introduced by Samuel Eilenberg and Saunders Mac Lane in
*General Theory of Natural Equivalences* (1945). They wanted to say precisely
what it means for an isomorphism to be *natural* — like the isomorphism between
a finite-dimensional vector space and its double dual, which (unlike the one
with its dual) needs no choice of basis. To define "natural transformation" they
needed "functor", and to define functor, "category". Grothendieck then made
categories the working language of algebraic geometry, and Lawvere proposed them
as a *foundation* for mathematics, rivalling set theory.

A **category** consists of objects and, for any two objects `X`, `Y`, a
collection of *morphisms* (arrows) `X ⟶ Y`, with identities `𝟙 X` and an
associative composition `f ≫ g` ("first `f`, then `g`"). That is all.
Nothing is said about what objects *are*: there is no membership relation, no
looking inside. An object is characterized only by its arrows to and from other
objects. This is the **structuralist** reading of mathematics (Benacerraf, Shapiro,
Awodey): mathematical objects are positions in structures, known through their
relations. In set-theoretic foundations, by contrast, the natural number `2` is a
particular set (`{∅, {∅}}` in von Neumann's coding of Part I), with "accidental"
properties such as `∅ ∈ 2`; categorically, `2` is known only up to unique
isomorphism, through its universal property.

A **functor** `F : C ⥤ D` maps objects to objects and arrows to arrows,
preserving identities and composition — a structure-preserving map of
structures. A **natural transformation** `α : F ⟶ G` is a family of arrows
`α_X : F X ⟶ G X` compatible with every arrow of `C`.

Examples in this file: the category of types and functions (Lean's own
"sets"); any preorder (at most one arrow `a ⟶ b`, namely the fact `a ≤ b`);
any monoid, and in particular any group, as a category with *one* object (the
arrows are the elements); the category of groups and homomorphisms from Part IV;
and the opposite of any category.

# The Yoneda lemma

*"Tell me who your friends are, and I will tell you who you are."* The Yoneda
lemma (Nobuo Yoneda, communicated to Mac Lane in a Paris railway station in
1954) is the precise form of the structuralist slogan that an object is
determined by its relations to all other objects.

To each object `A` of a category `C` corresponds its **hom-functor**
`Hom(A, −) : C ⥤ Type`, sending `X` to the type of arrows `A ⟶ X` — the
"view of the category from `A`". The lemma says that for every functor
`F : C ⥤ Type`,

  `Nat(Hom(A, −), F) ≅ F A`,

naturally in `A` and `F`: a natural transformation out of a hom-functor is
completely determined by where it sends the single element `𝟙 A`, and any element
of `F A` arises this way. The proof is almost nothing — yet the consequences are
everywhere:

* taking `F = Hom(B, −)` gives `Nat(Hom(B, −), Hom(A, −)) ≅ (A ⟶ B)`: the **Yoneda
  embedding** `A ↦ Hom(A, −)` is *fully faithful*; a category embeds faithfully into a
  category of functors (of "presheaves") without loss of information;
* hence **objects with naturally isomorphic hom-functors are isomorphic**: an object
  is determined, up to isomorphism, by the pattern of arrows out of it. Nothing
  "internal" remains to be known.

Grothendieck built on this the idea that a geometric space *is* the functor of
its points with values in all test spaces; universal properties, limits and
adjoints (the next files) are all instances of representability.

We also make functors and natural transformations into a category (the
**functor category**), so that the Yoneda embedding is itself a functor.

# Limits: products, terminal objects, equalisers, pullbacks

In set theory the cartesian product `X × Y` is a specific set of Kuratowski
pairs (Part I). Category theory replaces such constructions by **universal
properties**: a product of `X` and `Y` is *any* object `P` with arrows
`π₁ : P ⟶ X`, `π₂ : P ⟶ Y` through which every other such pair factors uniquely.
This says nothing about what `P` is made of — and that is the point. The
universal property determines `P` **up to unique isomorphism** (proved below for
each construction), which is exactly the degree of determinacy that mathematical
practice needs. Whether `(a, b)` "is" `{{a}, {a, b}}` becomes a non-question.

The same pattern gives:

* a **terminal object**: an object with exactly one arrow from every object (in
  types, the one-point type; in groups, the trivial group);
* the **equaliser** of two parallel arrows `f, g : X ⟶ Y`: the universal arrow
  `e : E ⟶ X` with `e ≫ f = e ≫ g` (in types, the subtype `{x | f x = g x}`);
* the **pullback** of a cospan `X ⟶ Z ⟵ Y`: the universal commutative square (in
  types, `{(x, y) | f x = g y}`, the fibre product).

All are instances of the general notion of a *limit* of a diagram, and by the
Yoneda philosophy a limit is a *representing object* for cones. We prove the
uniqueness theorems, and construct products, terminal objects, equalisers and
pullbacks of types, and products and terminal objects of groups.

# Adjunctions

*"Adjoint functors arise everywhere"* (Mac Lane). Daniel Kan introduced them in
1958; Lawvere made them the organising principle of logic and foundations. A
functor `F : C ⥤ D` is **left adjoint** to `G : D ⥤ C`, written `F ⊣ G`, when
arrows `F X ⟶ Y` in `D` correspond bijectively and naturally to arrows
`X ⟶ G Y` in `C`. Typically `G` forgets structure and `F` freely creates it:

* the **free monoid** on a type `α` is the type of lists `List α` under
  concatenation; a monoid homomorphism `List α ⟶ M` is the same thing as an
  arbitrary function `α → M` (its values on one-letter words). So
  *free ⊣ forgetful*;
* in the category of types, `(− × A) ⊣ (A → −)`: a function of two arguments is
  the same as a function returning functions — **currying** (Schönfinkel 1924,
  Curry). A category with products and such exponentials is **cartesian closed**;
  cartesian closed categories are the semantics of the simply typed λ-calculus of
  Part V (Lambek), another face of Curry–Howard.

Lawvere observed that the quantifiers of logic are adjoints too (`∃ ⊣ weakening ⊣ ∀`)
and that so is comprehension in set theory: adjunctions are where logic and
structure meet.

Every adjunction has a **unit** `η : 𝟭 ⟶ G F` and **counit** `ε : F G ⟶ 𝟭`
satisfying the *triangle identities*, and **right adjoints preserve limits** —
we prove it for terminal objects and binary products: the forgetful functor from
any algebraic category preserves products because it has a left adjoint.

# Lawvere's fixed-point theorem: the diagonal argument, once and for all

Cantor's theorem (no set maps onto its power set), Russell's paradox (there is
no set of all sets not containing themselves), Gödel's diagonal lemma (every
property of sentences has a "fixed point" sentence asserting it of itself),
Tarski's undefinability of truth, and Turing's unsolvability of the halting
problem — all are proved by a **diagonal argument**. In *Diagonal arguments and
cartesian closed categories* (1969) F. William Lawvere showed that they are all
instances of a single, almost trivial, theorem about categories with products:

> **Lawvere's fixed-point theorem.** If `φ : A × A ⟶ B` is *point-surjective* —
> every arrow `g : A ⟶ B` is `φ(a, −)` for some point `a` of `A` — then every
> endomorphism `t : B ⟶ B` has a fixed point.

Proof: apply the hypothesis to `g = t ∘ φ ∘ Δ` (where `Δ` is the diagonal
`x ↦ (x, x)`), obtaining a point `a` with `φ(a, x) = t(φ(x, x))` for all `x`;
then `b = φ(a, a)` satisfies `b = t(b)`. Read *contrapositively*, it is the
diagonal argument: if some `t` has **no** fixed point — negation on truth values,
`P ↦ ¬P`, or `b ↦ !b` on booleans — then **no** `φ` can be point-surjective:

* with `B = Prop` and `t = ¬`: no type surjects onto its power type `A → Prop`
  (**Cantor's theorem**; with `A` the "universe" and `φ = ∈` it is **Russell's
  paradox**, already met in `Paradoxes.lean` of Part I);
* with `B` the sentences of arithmetic and `φ` substitution: some sentence is
  equivalent to the negation of its own provability (**Gödel**; here `t` *does*
  have a fixed point, which is the content of the diagonal lemma);
* with `B = Bool` and `φ` the universal program: no program decides halting
  (**Turing**).

The paradoxes of self-reference are thus not about sets, sentences or machines as
such, but about the *structure* of self-application — a vindication of the
categorical point of view. We prove the theorem in an arbitrary category (with
"points" generalised to arrows out of any object `T`; classically `T` is the
terminal object), and derive Cantor's theorem for types from it.

# Part VII: Categories — structure itself

Categories, functors and natural transformations (Eilenberg–Mac Lane), with the
